title: Dementia patients warned off seeking home care in case Australia’s aged care algorithm cuts funding
author: Melissa Davey Medical editor
preview: Exclusive: FoI documents show senior health officials were warned of concerns about assessment tool weeks after it launched Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast People with dementia were warned not to apply for home support because of fears their care would be downgraded by the government’s aged care algorithm.
full_text_clean:
Home support can help prevent avoidable hospital admissions, deterioration and early entry into residential aged care. Photograph: Vithun Khamsong/Getty Images

Dementia patients warned off seeking home care in case Australia’s aged care algorithm cuts funding

Exclusive: FoI documents show senior health officials were warned of concerns about assessment tool weeks after it launched

People with dementia were warned not to apply for home support because of fears their care would be downgraded by the government’s aged care algorithm.

Documents released to Guardian Australia under freedom of information (FoI) laws reveal the warnings came within weeks of the November rollout of the algorithm, which is used to determine funding packages and priority of need for older Australians requiring home support.

Home support packages are critical to help prevent avoidable hospital admissions, deterioration and early entry into residential care.

Days before the algorithm was rolled out, the government barred aged care assessors from overriding the Integrated Assessment Tool’s (IAT) decisions, even if the level of funding and priority allocated were wrong or inadequate.

Dementia Australia wrote to senior health department staff on 8 December to say that since the addition of the algorithm, “We remain very concerned about the feedback we are receiving”.

The organisation cited the example of a man caring for his wife with dementia who was on a level three home care package, entitling her to around eight hours of support each week.

But her dementia had progressed and she needed to be reassessed so she could access additional care.

The woman’s husband was “advised by his local assessment service not to pursue a reassessment as they have seen a number of people with dementia receiving less or no support following IAT assessment, even if their care needs are increasing”.

The Older Persons Advocacy Network (Opan) sent a paper to department officials in February warning of deaths occurring due to the failing assessment system, and people with “extreme needs” being left without adequate support before their deaths.

“The inability of clinicians to intervene” and “over-reliance on automated decision-making is contributing to preventable deterioration and in some cases, death,” the document said.

In one example given by Opan, the algorithm refused a funding upgrade for a rapidly deteriorating person, forcing them to pay for private care despite the assessor’s view their existing package was grossly inadequate.

A senior health department staff member shared concerns ahead of a meeting between the department and advocacy groups in late December, the FoI documents show.

“Assessment orgs are telling [people] not to get an assessment as there is no guarantee they will get more funding,” the internal email read, adding that assessors were telling advocacy groups they had not been properly trained on the IAT.

title: Labor ditches new packaging laws to cut plastic waste, sparking unprecedented ‘scale and breadth of outrage’
author: Lisa Cox Environment and climate correspondent
preview: Federal environment department tells industry representatives the government does not want to ‘exacerbate cost of living pressures’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The Albanese government has been accused of breaking a promise after it shelved a longstanding commitment to bring in packaging standards intended to force manufacturers and retailers to cut plastic waste.
full_text_clean:
Environment minister Murray Watt (left) and prime minster Anthony Albanese. Labor says it will balance ‘environmental outcomes with the broader needs of the economy’ in the next term of government. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP

Labor ditches new packaging laws to cut plastic waste, sparking unprecedented ‘scale and breadth of outrage’

Federal environment department tells industry representatives the government does not want to ‘exacerbate cost of living pressures’

The Albanese government has been accused of breaking a promise after it shelved a longstanding commitment to bring in packaging standards intended to force manufacturers and retailers to cut plastic waste.

The federal environment department told industry representatives via email last week that the promise would not be kept before the next election because the government did not want to “exacerbate cost of living pressures”.

The director of the Boomerang Alliance, Jeff Angel, warned “ongoing inaction and token measures won’t be tolerated”.

“The Albanese government’s failure to act on packaging reform as promised is a repudiation of the public’s support of recycling and concerns about the health and environmental impacts of plastic pollution,” he said.

“The scale and breadth of outrage across a broad set of stakeholders from green groups to industry to state governments is something I have not seen before.”

The packaging laws had been under development since a 2023 agreement between the federal and state governments that the then environment minister, Tanya Plibersek, described as “historic”. They would have required producers to cut waste and boost plastics recycling.

Clean Up Australia’s annual litter reports highlight the persistent problem of packaging in the environment, with packaging accounting for 59.5% of all litter reported.

A suite of potential rules would have set design standards for packaging, for example by prohibiting use of certain chemicals, restricting unnecessary or excessive layers of packaging, or limiting the amount of empty space permitted within packaging.

Other potential changes could have required producers to be responsible for the packaging across its full life cycle – from the design stage to how the packaging is used and then disposed of.

The government’s decision to shelve its plans were due to its concern that any costs arising from changes could be passed on to consumers when they bought products such as groceries.

The department email said the environment minister, Murray Watt, wanted to pursue reforms “in a way that balances environmental outcomes with the broader needs of the economy, with the government looking closely at its policies to ensure it does not exacerbate cost of living pressures”.

The email said “a new Commonwealth scheme for packaging will not be introduced in this term of government” and the government would instead work with the states and territories “on opportunities to improve Australia’s packaging regulations and policies in the nearer term”.

The plastics campaign manager at the Australian Marine Conservation Society, Cip Hamilton, said the decision was “deeply disappointing”.

“Recyclers want action, businesses want certainty, and environmental organisations want an end to plastic pollution,” she said.

“Almost everyone was at the table, and the government has walked away.”

Hamilton said the laws would have “put the cost and the responsibility back where they belong – on the businesses using the packaging, not the households stuck with it”.

“Plastic pollution is having very real consequences. Little penguins are choking, seabirds are starving, and corals are suffocating,” she said.

Australian Packaging Covenant Organisation chief executive, Chris Foley, said producers wanted certainty. He said a national packaging regime with clear rules would “unlock investment in recycling, and replace fragmented approaches with a more consistent system”.

The chief executive of the Australian Council of Recycling, Suzanne Toumbourou, said the sector was calling for a “nationally consistent scheme with real targets”.

“We are already seeing recycling facilities close, with others under growing pressure, and the investment that built them go to waste, because there is no policy certainty to keep them viable,” she said.

Watt said the government understood that waste and recycling firms faced a range of challenges.

“The Albanese government is working closely with industry, and state and territory governments to strengthen the systems that support recycling, and improve the circularity, of Australia’s packaging,” he said.

“We’re committed to delivering stronger environmental outcomes while keeping costs to consumers and wider industry in check.”

He said the government’s immediate focus was to work with the states and territories to “reduce waste by harmonising packaging and recycling policy in Australia”.

title: One flight cancelled every three days due to staff shortages – as it happened
author: Achol Arok (now) and Nick Visser (earlier)
preview: This blog is now closed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast ‘Profound’ increase in death rate for welfare recipients, report finds People receiving an income support including disability, unemployment or carers payments had an average mortality rate more than nine times higher than people who did not access the welfare system, AAP reports.

One flight cancelled every three days due to staff shortages – as it happened

A Qantas plane passes an air traffic control tower in Sydney. Photograph: Hollie Adams/Reuters

Worker shortages have cancelled one flight every three days on average in the last year, Airservices Australia has told a Senate hearing.

The government agency’s deputy CEO, Peter Curran, said Australia’s airports recorded 2,536 cancellations over the year to 31 August, of which 121 were attributed to Airservices. Sydney accounted for 103 of those.

Just this morning, the troubled airport recorded 14 inbound cancellations and more outbound cancellations, after some overnight staff were unavailable, Curran said. Airservices and airlines manage the shortage by delaying or cancelling flights.

Curran said Sydney had grown and now needed a team of 41 air traffic controllers, spread across the roster. It has 49 employed but eight are unavailable at the moment. Curran said:

When we have a bit of short-term sickness or unavailability, like we had last night, it makes it very difficult to recover.

Curran said retired staff had been asked to come back to work but some of them were “simply not interested”. He said there were about 1,100 air traffic controllers working across Australia and 91 would join in the coming year.

With more recruitment, Curran said Airservices would be able to enough on-call staff to cover two absences a day by March 2027.

It’s not an ironclad model, but it certainly reduces the likelihood of the sorts of issues that we’re having today.

Planes on the tarmac at Sydney international airport. Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP

That’s a wrap on another eventful week in the news cycle.

Before we let you go, let’s recap the day’s top headlines:

Anthony Albanese has marked 25 years since the September 11 terrorist attacks in the US. Ten Australians were among 2,977 people killed in the terrorist attacks in New York, Washington DC and Pennsylvania – “lives tragically cut short far from home”.

The saga surrounding the One Nation cartoon labelling Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie a “traitor” continues as Pauline Hanson doubled down despite growing condemnation from all sides of parliament. Hastie said Barnaby Joyce had reached out to him with an explanation and apology, which he accepted.

The Victoria premier, Ben Carroll, joined in on the hype around the NFL game at the MCG this morning, calling it an exciting and historic day for the state.

Australia’s domestic spy agency said it has foiled 16 terrorist threats in the nine months since the Bondi attack, including an antisemitic attack.

Worker shortages have cancelled one flight every three days on average in the last year, Airservices Australia has told a Senate hearing.

That’s for sticking around, have a lovely weekend!

Roxanne Tickle welcomes rejection of Giggle’s appeal in landmark transgender discrimination case

The transgender woman at the centre of a successful discrimination case has welcomed the High Court’s rejection of an attempted appeal.

The High Court refused, with costs, an appeal by the women-only app Giggle against a Full Federal Court ruling in May. The ruling upheld a landmark decision that the app and its founder, Sall Grover, unlawfully discriminated against Roxanne Tickle after she was denied access to the platform.

It’s been nearly 5 years since I lodged my discrimination complaint. It’s been a relentlessly exhausting time, both physically and emotionally, for me and many others. I hope that yesterday’s High Court special leave refusal provides clarity to the protections in law for transgender and gender diverse people in Australia, and perhaps provides a beacon of light to the rest of the world. I wish my trans and gender diverse siblings, as well as their loved ones, much hope and love for their collective futures. May we all learn that just being different is not grounds for you to be ridiculed, attacked, feared or hated, but that instead you are providing a little something extra to the world. Life is not easy. Let’s all be kinder to each other and we might all enjoy it a little more.

Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson is being kept in near constant isolation, leaving her frightened and at risk of psychological decline, AAP reports.

A prisoner rights group is advocating on the triple murderer’s behalf for her to receive peer counselling to improve her mental wellbeing at no cost to the state.

Patterson’s current conditions at the Dame Phyllis Frost centre, west of Melbourne, involve being confined to a cell for a minimum of 22 hours a day and having approved contact with just one other prisoner through a wire mesh during limited yard time.

Advocacy group Justice Action has called the treatment tantamount to torture, invoking United Nations rules named after Nelson Mandela which say a person should not spend more that 15 consecutive days in solitary confinement.

The group is yet to be allowed direct contact with Patterson, but says information from other prisoners in the same unit suggests she is in a poor mental state.

Justice Action co-ordinator Brett Collins, who is a former inmate, said Patterson was entitled to be treated like any other prisoner and to serve her time constructively. He told AAP on Friday:

She’s a frightened woman, understandably so. She’s actually been now isolated for such a long time, and she’s already had those disorders before she before she was convicted, so now we’ve heard she’s unused to people being around her. That’s the sort of behaviour that causes causes permanent damages. It’s torture, actually.

She’s actually been now isolated for such a long time, and she’s already had those disorders before she before she was convicted, so now we’ve heard she’s unused to people being around her.

That’s the sort of behaviour that causes causes permanent damages. It’s torture, actually.

Justice Action is proposing Patterson be permitted a trained peer support mentor to help address and mitigate the psychiatric risks, which it would offer at no cost to taxpayers.

Major fire breaks out at building in Sydney’s north-west

Authorities are investigating the cause of a major building fire in Sydney’s north-west.

Emergency services responded to reports of the blaze on Loftus Street in Riverstone at around 1.35pm.

Fire and Rescue NSW said about 40 firefighters and 12 trucks remained at the scene. The fire has since been contained to the building where it started.

Four people were assessed at the scene, but none were taken to hospital.

Fire and Rescue NSW said the cause of the fire was under investigation.

Smoke billowing from the fire in Riverstone. Photograph: Nine News

Hello! I’ll be here to guide you through the rest of afternoon’s news.

That’s all for me. Achol Arok will take the blog from here. Take care!

An Australian Taxation Office employee has been charged with corruption-related offences by the AFP and other groups on allegations the man disclosed information obtained in his work to organised crime associates.

The AFP said today the Gold Coast man, 32, had been charged overnight with two counts of unlawfully disclosing information by a commonwealth officer. The offence carries a maximum penalty of two years in prison.

After a search warrant was carried out, the man was also charged with two counts of possession or control of child abuse material and 15 counts of using a carriage service for child abuse material. The maximum penalty for both offences is 15 years in prison.

Queensland’s credit rating downgraded for the first time in 17 years

Queensland has been dealt the first downgrade to its credit rating in 17 years, heaping more borrowing costs on to the state’s budget, AAP reports.

Credit agency S&P Global slapped a stable outlook on Queensland’s downgraded AA rating.

The loss of Queensland’s AA+ rating came on the same day NSW received an upgrade to its credit outlook. Queensland’s budget performance would remain “very weak” over the next two to three years compared to peers with a similar rating, S&P said on Friday.

The state’s historically large infrastructure program ahead of the 2032 Olympics and forecast deficits contrasted with previous expectations for sound surpluses from 2028, it said in a report.

The state could also expect lower stamp duty revenues after property tax changes in the federal budget exacerbated a deepening housing downturn, S&P said.

With more recruitment, Curran said Airservices would be able to enough on-call staff to cover two absences a day by March 2027.

It’s not an ironclad model, but it certainly reduces the likelihood of the sorts of issues that we’re having today.

Planes on the tarmac at Sydney international airport. Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP

Mike Evans, Demarcus Robinson and Deebo Samuel caught touchdown passes from quarterback Brock Purdy, and the San Francisco 49ers routed the Los Angeles Rams 27-7 Friday in the first NFL regular-season game in Australia.

Purdy passed for 205 yards against the Rams’ ineffective defense at the Melbourne Cricket Ground in front of 100,021 fans, the seventh-largest regular season crowd in NFL history.

Australia’s sporting capital reveled in its first real taste of American football – and in a dominant win by the 49ers, who had already won many Aussies’ affection by travelling to Melbourne a week earlier than the Rams, who only boomeranged in on Thursday morning.

NFL stars, cheerleaders and the Jonas Brothers as American football comes to Melbourne

About 100,000 fans filled the MCG for the historic NFL regular-season clash between the Los Angeles Rams and the San Francisco 49ers in Melbourne.

Die-hard supporters and interested spectators came from all corners to see American football’s cultural exchange, which included cheerleaders before the match and a Jonas Brothers show at half-time.

The Jonas Brothers perform at the half-time break. Photograph: Joel Carrett/EPA

San Francisco 49ers’ quarterback #13 Brock Purdy (R) runs with the ball during the NFL match. Photograph: Martin Keep/AFP/Getty Images

The Australian share market is barreling toward its worst week since the US-Iran war began, as surging oil prices pressure bond yields and squeeze central banks to hike borrowing costs.

The benchmark S&P/ASX200 index fell 112.2 points by midday on Friday, to be down 1.27% as the broader All Ordinaries tumbled 120 points, or 1.33%.

The top-200 is on track for a 3.2% slump since Monday and its worst week since early March’s 3.8% plunge, when US-led strikes killed Iran’s supreme leader and triggered a broader regional conflict.

The Australian dollar was buying 71.56 US cents, down from 72.16 US cents on Thursday at 5pm.

Emergency services responded to reports of the blaze on Loftus Street in Riverstone at around 1.35pm.

Four people were assessed at the scene, but none were taken to hospital.

Smoke billowing from the fire in Riverstone. Photograph: Nine News

Hello! I’ll be here to guide you through the rest of afternoon’s news.

That’s all for me. Achol Arok will take the blog from here. Take care!

An Australian Taxation Office employee has been charged with corruption-related offences by the AFP and other groups on allegations the man disclosed information obtained in his work to organised crime associates.

The AFP said today the Gold Coast man, 32, had been charged overnight with two counts of unlawfully disclosing information by a commonwealth officer. The offence carries a maximum penalty of two years in prison.

After a search warrant was carried out, the man was also charged with two counts of possession or control of child abuse material and 15 counts of using a carriage service for child abuse material. The maximum penalty for both offences is 15 years in prison.

Queensland’s credit rating downgraded for the first time in 17 years

Queensland has been dealt the first downgrade to its credit rating in 17 years, heaping more borrowing costs on to the state’s budget, AAP reports.

Credit agency S&P Global slapped a stable outlook on Queensland’s downgraded AA rating.

The loss of Queensland’s AA+ rating came on the same day NSW received an upgrade to its credit outlook. Queensland’s budget performance would remain “very weak” over the next two to three years compared to peers with a similar rating, S&P said on Friday.

The state’s historically large infrastructure program ahead of the 2032 Olympics and forecast deficits contrasted with previous expectations for sound surpluses from 2028, it said in a report.

Worker shortages have cancelled one flight every three days on average in the last year, Airservices Australia has told a Senate hearing.

Purdy passed for 205 yards against the Rams’ ineffective defense at the Melbourne Cricket Ground in front of 100,021 fans, the seventh-largest regular season crowd in NFL history.

Australia’s sporting capital reveled in its first real taste of American football – and in a dominant win by the 49ers, who had already won many Aussies’ affection by travelling to Melbourne a week earlier than the Rams, who only boomeranged in on Thursday morning.

About 100,000 fans filled the MCG for the historic NFL regular-season clash between the Los Angeles Rams and the San Francisco 49ers in Melbourne.

Die-hard supporters and interested spectators came from all corners to see American football’s cultural exchange, which included cheerleaders before the match and a Jonas Brothers show at half-time.

The benchmark S&P/ASX200 index fell 112.2 points by midday on Friday, to be down 1.27% as the broader All Ordinaries tumbled 120 points, or 1.33%.

title: Australian fuel prices set to rise by 30c as global markets react to ‘deadly cocktail’
author: Patrick Commins Economics editor
preview: Global oil price at its highest since May while investors dump stocks and bonds after Donald Trump’s $5,000 ‘dividend’ promise Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Fuel prices are on track to climb a further 20-30 cents per litre over the coming weeks, after the escalating Middle East conflict pushed the global oil...
full_text_clean:
Australian fuel prices are on track to climb 30 cents in coming weeks as the Middle East conflict pushes the global oil price to its highest since mid-May. Photograph: Asanka Ratnayake/Getty Images

Australian fuel prices set to rise by 30c as global markets react to ‘deadly cocktail’

Global oil price at its highest since May while investors dump stocks and bonds after Donald Trump’s $5,000 ‘dividend’ promise

Fuel prices are on track to climb a further 20-30 cents per litre over the coming weeks, after the escalating Middle East conflict pushed the global oil price to its highest since mid-May.

As investors dumped stocks and bonds in an increasingly febrile environment, Donald Trump’s promise to give every US adult citizen a US$5,000 “dividend” after the November midterms if Republicans win added to alarm around the parlous state of the country’s finances.

Investors pushed US bond yields towards 5% for the first time since 2007 as the prospect of higher energy costs firmed up expectations that the US Federal Reserve would need to hike rates again.

That dragged Australia’s 10-year rate up to 5.38% and to fresh 15-year highs.

The international oil benchmark, Brent crude, pushed towards US$110 a barrel, before settling at above US$108 in late Friday trade.

Steve Miller, an investment strategist at fund manager GSFM, said bonds were reacting to a “deadly cocktail” of high oil prices, American fiscal irresponsibility, and worries around the independence of the Fed.

“The $5,000 promise is a great example of Trump’s unwillingness to tackle the deficit, and even to make it worse for short-term political expediency. No wonder bond markets are sketchy,” Miller said.

Tai Hui, chief market strategist for Asia-Pacific at JP Morgan Asset Management, said rising long-term borrowing rates would normally undermine stock valuations, as investors rethink the relative trade-off between the riskier sharemarket and climbing yields on safe bonds.

Evidence of this was clear on the ASX this week, where the benchmark S&P/ASX 200 index was on track to end the week down 3% and below the level it was this time last year.

But Hui said ongoing optimism about the state of the global economy and, especially, the titanic boom in artificial intelligence investment was providing a tailwind for sharemarkets around the world, and especially on Wall Street.

Since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran at the end of February, the US benchmark S&P 500 sharemarket index is up about 10%, against a 5% fall for the ASX 200.

But the Hong Kong-based Hui said the increasingly debated question among investors was at what point the steady march higher in yields begins to drive a broader and deeper switch out of stocks and into bonds.

As economists warned of a new post-Covid era of structurally higher interest rates, financial markets upped their bets that the Reserve Bank of Australia would deliver a fourth rate hike on 29 September, pricing in an 80% chance.

Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, said the RBA would have to respond to recent evidence that inflationary pressures were not easing as hoped, even as the economy proved resilient.

“I think they [the RBA] will go in September,” Kearns said.

The former top RBA official said the central bank’s inflation-fighting credentials were increasingly at stake.

“They need to get inflation to 2.5%, and that’s not forecast to happen until early 2028; that then becomes almost a seven-year inflationary episode.”

The prospect of higher mortgage costs comes as Vivek Dhar, CBA’s head of commodities research, warned that diesel prices could climb by 10-30 cents per litre over the coming weeks, from over $2.50 per litre today.

Unleaded petrol prices could push from about $2.10 a litre in major east coast cities to about $2.30 over the next couple of weeks, according to a rough rule of thumb that says every US$1 increase in the crude oil benchmark translates to a 10c increase at the pump.

Dhar, who is based in Singapore, said meetings with energy producers and traders on the sidelines of a major energy conference over recent days revealed a deep sense of uncertainty about how the next six to 12 months will play out.

Dhar said he expected Brent crude to swing between US$70 and US$100 a barrel for the foreseeable future, until eventually the world becomes comfortable with the supply workarounds to a restricted strait of Hormuz.

But the more pressing worries were around the supply of refined products, particularly diesel.

“Everyone pays attention to oil, but it’s the refined product that hits the economy and feeds through to inflation. And that is what everyone is worried about, because there isn’t any workaround; we just need disruptions to stop.”

title: NSW police settle trespass case after visiting Indigenous children’s home 150 times in 20 months
author: Australian Associated Press
preview: Trespass case launched by two mothers settled after officers often went to families’ houses between midnight and 4am Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Two Indigenous mothers have settled a trespass case against New South Wales police, after officers turned up at one of their homes 150 times in 20 months to...
full_text_clean:
NSW police settled the case after officers attended a woman’s home more than 150 times over 20 months, including at night. Composite: Victoria Hart/Guardian Design/Getty Images

NSW police settle trespass case after visiting Indigenous children’s home 150 times in 20 months

Trespass case launched by two mothers settled after officers often went to families’ houses between midnight and 4am

Two Indigenous mothers have settled a trespass case against New South Wales police, after officers turned up at one of their homes 150 times in 20 months to conduct bail checks on her sons.

The case, which was launched against NSW police in April 2024, was settled on confidential terms three weeks before it was to go to trial in the supreme court.

One of the complainants, a single mum who uses the pseudonym Megan for privacy, has two sons, who were on bail from the ages of 11 and 13 after being found as passengers in a stolen car.

Police attended her home in regional NSW more than 150 times over 20 months, with many of the visits taking place between midnight and 4am.

NSW legislation allows courts to authorise police to attend a private residence to check that someone is complying with their bail conditions.

But the Justice and Equity Centre, representing Megan in court, argued that many of the bail checks were done without court authorisation, which amounted to trespass.

Megan said the visits often involved police banging on doors, shining torches through the windows and letting themselves in through the back gate in the middle of the night.

She said the visits were scary and stressful for her family and resulted in her kids missing school because of exhaustion.

‘‘My eldest is driving around with his head held high now, knowing police can’t just randomly pull him over,’’ Megan said.

‘‘But I know he’s still shaking in fear about what they could do.

‘‘They’ve already done the damage, and it will take a lot for my boys to start trusting police again.”

The other complainant, a single mum of three who uses the pseudonym Joanne, said police visited her western Sydney home to do bail checks on her son more than 90 times in 18 months.

She said in the space of a few hours, police conducted three such checks.

“The checks often happened on school nights, which meant my youngest daughter was too tired to go to school in the morning,” she said.

NSW police said the officers were acting lawfully when they conducted the bail compliance checks.

A police spokesperson said such checks were an important tool for keeping the public safe and managing risks associated with letting people out of jail during an ongoing court process.

But a report from the state’s Law Enforcement Conduct Commission, released in 2025, found police were stretching their authority and powers by relying on a weak legal principle to conduct bail compliance checks without court authorisation.

The mothers’ solicitor, Kate Sinclair, said it was immensely brave for her clients to bring the case against the force.

‘‘They did it for their families and their communities and we respect their courage,’’ she said.

Megan and her sons have separately taken NSW police to the federal court for racial discrimination, arguing that the boys were targeted because they are Aboriginal.

title: ‘Absurd, hardline calls’: questions over Sweden’s post-Brexit migration policy
author: Lisa O’Carroll in Stockholm
preview: Sweden has ordered more Britons, including vulnerable people, to leave post-Brexit than any other EU country He arrived with nothing other than the clothes he wore that morning. Hours later he was banged up in a detention centre close to a Stockholm airport to await deportation.
full_text_clean:
Questions are mounting as to why Sweden appears to have taken such a hardline approach to the Brexit withdrawal agreement over migration. Photograph: Wdnet Studio/Alamy

‘Absurd, hardline calls’: questions over Sweden’s post-Brexit migration policy

Sweden has ordered more Britons, including vulnerable people, to leave post-Brexit than any other EU country

He arrived with nothing other than the clothes he wore that morning. Hours later he was banged up in a detention centre close to a Stockholm airport to await deportation.

Charles, a former business director from Cambridge, who did not want his full name published, moved to Sweden in 2017 to be with his Swedish wife, Lily, and applied to remain after Brexit, before the deadline of December 2021.

But the migration agency rejected his application, and he and his wife have been fighting with the Swedish authorities ever since.

In a message passed on by Lily, he said he was the only Briton in the detention centre, where he described being hemmed in by three lines of fences separated by a “no man’s land”.

“I arrived here with nothing apart from the clothes I had on,” Charles said. “We were told the meeting … with the border police was to discuss my case. They then said they thought I would abscond, which is why they were going to detain me.”

Lily, a lawyer, questioned whether Sweden, considered a global leader in human rights and progressive politics, was now like Afghanistan. “They have hunted us for five years,” she said.

Charles could be deported in the next week unless his latest legal challenge delivers a reprieve.

He joins a list of 2,490 Britons – of an estimated 14,000 in Sweden – deported from the country between 2020 and 2025, as questions are mounting as to why Sweden appears to have taken such a hardline approach to the Brexit withdrawal agreement (WA) over migration.

In total, Sweden is responsible for 33% of all British nationals deported from the EU between 2021 and 2025, compared with France, which accounted for 6% of all British deportees, Spain at 3% and Germany at 2%. France deported 450, Spain 250 and Germany 160, while Italy deported just 15 Britons in that period.

Different countries collate data in different ways, but Eurostat data suggests the Netherlands is another outlier, with 2,270 Britons deported in the same period.

Data shows 2,100 removal orders were also issued in Sweden, though it is not clear how many of these resulted in voluntary departures or progressed to deportations.

Joyce Thomas, 78, walks her dog just hours before she is due to be ‘removed’ from Sweden after 22 years. Photograph: Lisa O’Carroll

People served with removal orders include Joyce Thomas, a 78-year-old widow who has been in Sweden for 22 years, and George Mason, a 74-year-old with dementia who has been in Sweden for 25 years, both of whose applications missed the deadline to apply to remain in Sweden post-Brexit.

John Sellers, a 34-year-old Briton who has lived in Sweden since he was 10, was deported in January.

The cases also raise the question of whether the WA delivers the political promise made by the Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier and others promising citizens should not be collateral damage of Brexit.

“The level of protection afforded under EU law must not be watered down. Brexit should not alter the nature of people’s daily lives,” Barnier said in 2017.

Nine years on, some have asked if Sweden’s approach has been infected by its apparent lurch to the right more broadly, serving deportations on children and even a 95-year-old Iraqi woman who had lived in Sweden for 20 years.

“The number of absurd, hardline calls from the migration department just keeps piling up,” the Swedish author and journalist Martin Gelin wrote this week ahead of the general election on Sunday.

British citizens who lived in the country before Brexit have unique protection under the WA, but activists have noted that they appear to be subject to the same treatment as other foreign nationals.

George Mason, 74, seen here with his daughter Michelle, has been served with a removal notice. Photograph: The Mason family

“The question is, has national migration policy affected the way in which they apply the withdrawal agreement in edge cases? And has it affected the culture in Migrationsverket [the migration agency] and perhaps in the courts as they apply the withdrawal agreement?” asked James Savage, the editor of the Local, which recently revealed the pressure applied to Sweden by the European Commission.

Family members acting on behalf of Mason turned to the general migration route for residency after the migration agency rejected the withdrawal agreement request for him to remain in the country. The judge’s ruling was clear: “The state’s interest in regulated immigration outweighs Horace [George] Mason’s interest in continuing to reside [in Sweden].”

Since the surge in publicity surrounding deportations of British citizens in Sweden, all three opposition parties have pledged new laws to reopen the application process for Britons, and the incumbent government has said it would look at doing the same.

Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for the Centre party, has promised new laws if his party retains power. “Some of these cases are just stupid,” he told the Guardian. “They [the migration agency] should not be lenient, but the present decision-making leans towards deportation.”

The Swedish migration agency insists it has only deported 458 British people in strict Brexit-related cases but activists – who have been trying to get granular detail on the remaining cases – say that data may not include Britons who upon rejection from the agency then applied to stay under different routes and ended up with deportation orders.

The agency also says there is “no indication that Sweden has in any way interpreted the withdrawal agreement in an extreme manner or differently from other [EU] member states” and that it has “applied applicable law” with appeal processes.

Savage notes that promises to change the law were made three years ago after other cases emerged.

David Milstead, who runs the activist group Brits in Sweden, has welcomed promises of action but is concerned that politicians might provide a fix for future British applicants without giving a second chance to those already deported or who have left voluntarily.

A spokesperson for the European Commission said: “Correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement is very important to us,” but added: “Reasonable grounds that may justify a late application for beneficiary status are not defined in the withdrawal agreement.”

This means “host states have a certain margin of discretion in deciding what they accept as reasonable grounds”.

‘Some of these cases are just stupid,’ said Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for the Centre party. Photograph: Centerpartie, Sweden

In other words, Sweden has not breached the withdrawal agreement but rather is exercising allowable discretion.

Catherine Barnard, a professor of EU law at Cambridge University, says the withdrawal agreement is “unique”, as no other member state has ever left the EU, and will take time to test. But decisions by migration authorities have to be proven to be “proportionate”.

While Swedish courts have not referred their decision-making upwards to the European court of justice, Barnard says a case in the UK may provide precedent for EU citizens affected by the WA.

In the case of “CG”, the European court of justice ruled that the UK breached the EU charter of fundamental rights in denying benefits to an EU citizen in Northern Ireland.

“In a 2021 case … the court ruled that the charter would apply to those who had moved to another member state before Brexit and lived there,” Barnard said.

“While the facts of the case were somewhat different, the principle should remain: the state’s interest in protecting its immigration must be balanced against the rights to family life of vulnerable individuals.”

The Swedish migration authorities and police have been approached for comment on the detention of Charles.

Joyce Thomas, 78, walks her dog just hours before she is due to be ‘removed’ from Sweden after 22 years. Photograph: Lisa O’Carroll

People served with removal orders include Joyce Thomas, a 78-year-old widow who has been in Sweden for 22 years, and George Mason, a 74-year-old with dementia who has been in Sweden for 25 years, both of whose applications missed the deadline to apply to remain in Sweden post-Brexit.

John Sellers, a 34-year-old Briton who has lived in Sweden since he was 10, was deported in January.

The cases also raise the question of whether the WA delivers the political promise made by the Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier and others promising citizens should not be collateral damage of Brexit.

“The level of protection afforded under EU law must not be watered down. Brexit should not alter the nature of people’s daily lives,” Barnier said in 2017.

Nine years on, some have asked if Sweden’s approach has been infected by its apparent lurch to the right more broadly, serving deportations on children and even a 95-year-old Iraqi woman who had lived in Sweden for 20 years.

“The number of absurd, hardline calls from the migration department just keeps piling up,” the Swedish author and journalist Martin Gelin wrote this week ahead of the general election on Sunday.

British citizens who lived in the country before Brexit have unique protection under the WA, but activists have noted that they appear to be subject to the same treatment as other foreign nationals.

George Mason, 74, seen here with his daughter Michelle, has been served with a removal notice. Photograph: The Mason family

“The question is, has national migration policy affected the way in which they apply the withdrawal agreement in edge cases? And has it affected the culture in Migrationsverket [the migration agency] and perhaps in the courts as they apply the withdrawal agreement?” asked James Savage, the editor of the Local, which recently revealed the pressure applied to Sweden by the European Commission.

Family members acting on behalf of Mason turned to the general migration route for residency after the migration agency rejected the withdrawal agreement request for him to remain in the country. The judge’s ruling was clear: “The state’s interest in regulated immigration outweighs Horace [George] Mason’s interest in continuing to reside [in Sweden].”

Since the surge in publicity surrounding deportations of British citizens in Sweden, all three opposition parties have pledged new laws to reopen the application process for Britons, and the incumbent government has said it would look at doing the same.

Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for the Centre party, has promised new laws if his party retains power. “Some of these cases are just stupid,” he told the Guardian. “They [the migration agency] should not be lenient, but the present decision-making leans towards deportation.”

The Swedish migration agency insists it has only deported 458 British people in strict Brexit-related cases but activists – who have been trying to get granular detail on the remaining cases – say that data may not include Britons who upon rejection from the agency then applied to stay under different routes and ended up with deportation orders.

The agency also says there is “no indication that Sweden has in any way interpreted the withdrawal agreement in an extreme manner or differently from other [EU] member states” and that it has “applied applicable law” with appeal processes.

Savage notes that promises to change the law were made three years ago after other cases emerged.

David Milstead, who runs the activist group Brits in Sweden, has welcomed promises of action but is concerned that politicians might provide a fix for future British applicants without giving a second chance to those already deported or who have left voluntarily.

A spokesperson for the European Commission said: “Correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement is very important to us,” but added: “Reasonable grounds that may justify a late application for beneficiary status are not defined in the withdrawal agreement.”

This means “host states have a certain margin of discretion in deciding what they accept as reasonable grounds”.

‘Some of these cases are just stupid,’ said Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for the Centre party. Photograph: Centerpartie, Sweden

In other words, Sweden has not breached the withdrawal agreement but rather is exercising allowable discretion.

Catherine Barnard, a professor of EU law at Cambridge University, says the withdrawal agreement is “unique”, as no other member state has ever left the EU, and will take time to test. But decisions by migration authorities have to be proven to be “proportionate”.

While Swedish courts have not referred their decision-making upwards to the European court of justice, Barnard says a case in the UK may provide precedent for EU citizens affected by the WA.

In the case of “CG”, the European court of justice ruled that the UK breached the EU charter of fundamental rights in denying benefits to an EU citizen in Northern Ireland.

“In a 2021 case … the court ruled that the charter would apply to those who had moved to another member state before Brexit and lived there,” Barnard said.

“While the facts of the case were somewhat different, the principle should remain: the state’s interest in protecting its immigration must be balanced against the rights to family life of vulnerable individuals.”

The Swedish migration authorities and police have been approached for comment on the detention of Charles.

title: Ireland holds its breath as its leftwing president prepares to meet Trump
author: Rory Carroll Ireland correspondent
preview: Many are rooting for vocal critic Catherine Connolly to let rip in Dublin meeting, but others hope she holds back Catherine Connolly, Ireland’s president, once said she abhorred Donald Trump’s policies. In his sole previous comment on Connolly, the US president seemed to think she was a man. Now that they are about to meet, Ireland is holding its breath.
full_text_clean:
Ireland’s government is said to be anxious about Donald Trump’s meeting with Catherine Connolly at Áras an Uachtaráin, the Irish president’s official residence. Composite: Reuters

Ireland holds its breath as its leftwing president prepares to meet Trump

Many are rooting for vocal critic Catherine Connolly to let rip in Dublin meeting, but others hope she holds back

Catherine Connolly, Ireland’s president, once said she abhorred Donald Trump’s policies. In his sole previous comment on Connolly, the US president seemed to think she was a man. Now that they are about to meet, Ireland is holding its breath.

Trump is to fly into Dublin on Saturday morning for a two-day visit centred on golf. But before making it to his beloved greens, protocol obliges him to meet a woman who has given every impression of loathing him.

A courtesy call to Áras an Uachtaráin, the Irish president’s official residence and workplace in the city’s Phoenix Park, has left the government anxious and the media reaching for popcorn. “What could possibly go wrong?” headlines ask.

Many in Ireland are rooting for Connolly to let rip at Trump for his policies and rhetoric on immigrants and the Middle East. Others hope she will stifle any criticisms to avoid provoking a visitor who could upend Ireland’s economy.

The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said he had no concerns “at all” about the encounter, but one senior official said the government was on tenterhooks. “We need to get him [Trump] in the Áras, then out of the Áras. We’ll breathe easier after,” they said.

As MP, Connolly protested Trump’s 2019 visit to Ireland and more recently assailed him over his positions and policies on Gaza, Iran and other issues. Photograph: Niall Carson/PA

Before winning the Irish presidency – a ceremonial post – last year, Connolly was an independent leftwing member of parliament for Galway who protested against Trump’s 2019 visit and more recently assailed him over his positions and policies on Gaza, Iran and other issues. “If we are going to act as an independent sovereign state, a neutral republic, we must use our voice to speak to power and the abuse of power by president Trump,” she said.

Asked in March about the criticism, Trump replied: “He’s lucky I exist.”

Trump is now to meet Connolly – and Martin in a separate meeting – before heading to his golf resort in Doonbeg, County Clare, which is hosting the Irish Open.

Heavy security around the Phoenix Park and Doonbeg will insulate the US president from protests, including a “No welcome for Trump” demonstration that is expected to draw thousands to central Dublin on Saturday afternoon.

Garda officers patrol the beach at the Irish Open in Doonbeg before Donald Trump’s expected arrival at the weekend. Photograph: Brian Lawless/PA

Some hope Connolly will speak for them when she meets Trump behind closed doors. “She should speak truth to power,” Rosie O’Donnell, the US comedian who moved to Ireland after Trump won a second term, told the Irish Independent. “I don’t think she should drop what she believes in to be polite to a madman. He is like a mad king that has destroyed the country.”

Leftwing parties that supported Connolly’s presidential run urged the former barrister to “find a way” to convey criticism without causing a diplomatic storm. Trump has expressed affection for the emerald isle but also wants American tech and pharmaceutical firms to move jobs and taxes from Ireland to the US, a scenario that could devastate Irish state finances.

During her election campaign, Connolly promised to heed constraints of the office, which is largely symbolic and has no responsibility for foreign policy. She also said that if asked, she would meet Trump.

“That implies that it’s not to meet him in order to berate him,” said Bobby McDonagh, an former Irish ambassador to the UK and EU. “She’ll have an opportunity to have a chat with President Trump and make some gentle points reflective of Irish values. I expect it to go smoothly.”

Connolly could emulate Martin, who discreetly rebutted some of Trump’s opinions during a visit to the White House, said McDonagh. “He had the emotional intelligence and experience to do it in a way that didn’t provoke any reaction.”

The six-time major champion golfer Rory McIlroy said he and other competitors at Doonbeg would focus on the game, not politics. “It’s going to be different with him being here but we’re here to play a golf tournament and it’s a good golf course so we’ll keep our heads down and play,” McIlroy said.

title: AfD’s new state MPs include ex-Stasi officer, former porn actor, neopagans and neo-Nazis
author: Kate Connolly in Berlin
preview: Far-right German party’s newly elected representatives face fresh scrutiny as it tries to form government in Saxony-Anhalt • Why is the AfD’s state victory significant and what might happen next?
full_text_clean:
The AfD’s parliamentary group leader in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, referred to the MPs under criminal investigation as ‘the bad guys’. Photograph: Karina Hessland/Reuters

AfD’s new state MPs include ex-Stasi officer, former porn actor, neopagans and neo-Nazis

Far-right German party’s newly elected representatives face fresh scrutiny as it tries to form government in Saxony-Anhalt

The Alternative für Deutschland is facing scrutiny over the suitability of some of its prospective new MPs – including a former Stasi officer and a former pornography actor – just days after its historic win in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Presented by the AfD’s lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, for a photocall in the state capital of Magdeburg on Thursday, some of the members-elect were revealed to have a range of questionable backgrounds, including criminal records, Stasi pasts and connections to far-right networks.

The AfD’s newly elected members of the Saxony-Anhalt parliament. Photograph: Karina Hessland/Reuters

German media has revealed that among the 39 parliamentarians who will represent constituencies across Saxony-Anhalt in the state parliament, is a man alleged to have participated in pornography films and falsified academic qualifications; a former officer for the East German secret police, the Stasi; and several members under criminal investigation for their involvement in neo-Nazi organisations.

Two MPs are facing investigations into allegations they sought to continue the activities of the banned rightwing extremist organisation Artgemeinschaft, a neopagan group that has embraced nationalist and antisemitic ideas. The younger of the two is also alleged to have violated the law in relation to weapons, according to the public prosecutor’s office. Both reject the allegations.

The erstwhile pornography actor was convicted for stealing bedding in bulk from a hotel. A court confirmed he had been a pornography actor after he contested a local newspaper’s claims. He was expelled from a university after being found to have falsified his school leaving certificate, Die Zeit reported. The MP says he was readmitted after a legal challenge.

An ex-Stasi officer, aged 78, who won a direct mandate in his constituency, has admitted to having worked for the ministry for state security in the communist GDR, focused on East German citizens who wanted to permanently emigrate.

His role as an MP-elect has been criticised by campaign groups on behalf of victims of the former East German dictatorship.

Also, an investigation by the broadcaster ZDF revealed that some AfD ministers-elect who were also members of the previous parliamentary group, had ties to rightwing extremist groups. This included some having been members of the subsequently outlawed Homeland-Loyal German Youth group, HDJ. At one stage one of them had led the organisation, while an adviser to the AfD’s parliamentary group wrote a biography described as an “homage to national socialism”.

Among the prospective MPs are a number with pro-Kremlin links, as well as some who visited members of the Maga movement in Washington.

Asked to respond to the questionable biographies, in particular of the two MPs under criminal investigation, Siegmund, a former fragrance salesman who was unanimously re-elected as the AfD’s parliamentary group leader on Thursday, referred to the men in jest as “the bad guys” and said “we will await the results of the investigations and then discuss them”.

Ulrich Siegmund at the AfD election party after polls closed last Sunday. Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters

Siegmund himself triggered fierce criticism during the presentation of his new parliamentary group after linking the production of arms in Germany to the party’s planned deportation offensive.

In response to a journalist’s question about the planned opening of an Israeli arms company in the state, Siegmund said: “We do not categorically condemn the production of arms, because we will of course need equivalent resources for the future remigration and deportation offensive. This is also in the interest of internal security, our own instability and national defence.”

The statement was seized on by the party’s opponents. Katja Pähle, the chair of the Social Democrats (SPD) parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt, said Siegmund had issued a “political threat” by suggesting the use of “violence as a political tool”.

“This reveals the ugly face of a political system whose language and ideas are once again reminiscent of totalitarian models,” she said.

Whether the AfD, which secured 44% of the seats, forms a state government, which would make it the first far-right party to gain power in Germany since the second world war, will depend on whether it can find other like-minded MPs who might defect, or a single party willing to support the AfD. So far, the mainstream parties have refused to enter a coalition with the AfD, which has just under half of the 83 seats in the state, three short of an absolute majority.

Protests against the AfD are planned in more than 20 cities across Germany this weekend in response to the party’s win last Sunday, and ahead of two crucial state elections on 20 September, in Berlin and in Mecklenburg Vorpommen, where the AfD are predicted to do well.

title: Sweden’s PM channels Trump saying he wants to ‘make Sweden great again’ ahead of election – as it happened
author: Jakub Krupa (now and earlier) and Martin Belam (earlier)
preview: Ulf Kristersson’s comments come ahead of the parliamentary election taking place this Sunday in Brussels The European Commission has said it is assessing whether Ukraine has a funding shortfall, amid renewed pressure to use Russia’s frozen assets to aid Kyiv. “That [frozen assets] is not a primary focus.
full_text_clean:
Sweden’s PM channels Trump saying he wants to ‘make Sweden great again’ ahead of election – as it happened

Ulf Kristersson’s comments come ahead of the parliamentary election taking place this Sunday

Prime minister Ulf Kristersson speaking to the press earlier today. Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters

Channeling his Donald Trump spirit, Sweden’s prime minister Ulf Kristersson told AFP that he hoped to secure a second term in this Sunday’s parliamentary election to “make Sweden great again.”

Prime minister Ulf Kristersson talks to members of the media after a Moderate Party rally ahead of the general election in Stockholm, Sweden. Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters

Kristersson has led a three-party centre-right coalition since 2022, which relies on outside support from the far-right Sweden Democrats. If the right bloc wins, the party is expected to join the government for the first time in history.

But polls suggest that a centre-left opposition bloc of former PM Magdalena Andersson is slightly ahead, with a combined 50.8% of vote share, compared to 47.6% for the centre-right and far-right parties.

The vote on Sunday is expected to be very close, and it may take weeks before we know who will form the next government as political talks are likely to be fraught and take time.

And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.

Sweden’s prime minister Ulf Kristersson told AFP that he hoped to secure a second term in this Sunday’s parliamentary election to “make Sweden great again,” as the country entered final hours of campaigning ( 14:23).

The latest polls ahead of the vote show narrowing gap between the two main blocs, potentially complicating the government-formation process after Sunday ( 15:34, 17:01).

The leaders of the eight main political parties will tonight face off in the final televised debate, with the economy, education, climate, integration and healthcare among the topics on the table ( 14:57).

We will cover the Swedish election night on Europe Live on Sunday night, live from Stockholm.

At least two people were killed and 12 injured in Russian strikes on two petrol stations in Kyiv on Friday morning as the bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters a new phase of intensity ( 9:48, 11:17, 13:47, 16:09).

If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.

I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.

Back to Sweden, where the Social Democrat leader, Magdalena Andersson, told the Swedish broadcaster SVT that “the bloc differences will decrease as we approach election day, I have predicted that for a long time.”

She was responding to a yet another new poll showing the gap between the two groups narrowing, with just over 48 hours to go until the polls close.

SVT/Verian’s poll says Social Democrats will win with 27.6% of the vote, ahead of the far-right Sweden Democrats at 18.1% and the Moderates at 15.8%.

Petrol stations in Kyiv have been hit by jet-powered drones in a wave of targeted Russian attacks as the bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters a new phase of intensity.

At least two people were killed and 12 injured in strikes on two petrol stations on Friday morning, according to the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko.

The rush-hour strikes follow a similar attack on a petrol station on Thursday, the first of its kind in the capital.

At the Ukrnafta petrol station in the Pochaina neighbourhood in northern Kyiv, bystanders said three people had been injured in Friday’s blast – the manager of a nearby car wash, his wife and the driver of a passing car. The blown-out vehicle was stranded by the side of the road, its windows shattered and seats spattered in blood.

Witnesses said they had heard two explosions, and local authorities later said Russia had carried out a double-tap attack on the facility.

Pochaina petrol station in Kyiv, Ukraine. Photograph: Amy Hawkins

“This is probably one of the most difficult periods of the war because life is just like on a rollercoaster,” said Anastasiia Demchenko, 30, who works at a delivery company opposite the petrol station. “It feels like life is on the edge.”

All three strikes targeted petrol stations operated by Ukrnafta, a state-owned oil and natural gas extraction company.

Sergiy Fedorenko, the acting head of Naftogaz, Ukrnafta’s parent company, said: “There is, and can be, no military objective behind such attacks. This is terror directed at the civilian population, at peaceful people.”

Let’s go back to Ukraine and get you the latest from our correspondent, Amy Hawkins, in Kyiv.

Highlighting just how close the margins are likely to be on Sunday, the latest DN/Ipsos poll shows a difference of just… 0.3 percentage points between the centre-left and the centre-right to far-right blocs.

If confirmed, it would give the opposition 175 seats in the new parliament, just one more than the current government.

Magdalena Andersson, former prime minister of Sweden, speaks during an event in Barcelona, Spain, earlier this year. Photograph: Nacho Doce/Reuters

Later tonight, the leaders of the eight main political parties will face off in the final televised debate ahead of Sunday’s vote.

Christian Democrats party leader Ebba Busch (KD), Green Party spokesperson Amanda Lind (MP), Sweden Democrats party leader Jimmie Akesson (SD), Social Democrats party leader Magdalena Andersson (S) and Moderates party leader Ulf Kristersson (M) in the studio ahead of TV4's election debate in Stockholm, Sweden yesterday. Photograph: Anders Wiklund/TT/Reuters

The discussion will focus on the economy, education, climate, integration and healthcare, according to the Swedish public broadcaster SVT.

SVT somewhat proudly noted that it has a history in hosting the final debates in each race, going back to 1960.

While the Swedish campaign focused on a range of issues including Sweden’s welfare state, immigration and crime, there was no single dominant issue, experts said.

A man sits on a bench in front of election campaign posters for Sweden's Social Democratic party and Moderate Party in central Stockholm, Sweden. Photograph: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP/Getty Images

“Nothing has really stuck, it’s been sort of unsatisfactory in that ⁠sense,” Nicholas Aylott, an associate professor at Södertörn University, told Reuters.

The centre-left opposition looked set to win, albeit ​by a narrower margin than seen in polls during ​early summer, Aylott said.

title: Russia targets Kyiv petrol stations for first time with jet-powered drones
author: Amy Hawkins in Kyiv
preview: Three facilities in two days struck as bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters new phase of intensity Europe live – latest updates Petrol stations in Kyiv have been hit by jet-powered drones in a wave of targeted Russian attacks as the bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters a new phase of intensity.

The aftermath of a Russian drone strike on one of two petrol stations targeted on Friday. Photograph: Alina Smutko/Reuters

Russia targets Kyiv petrol stations for first time with jet-powered drones

Three facilities in two days struck as bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters new phase of intensity

Petrol stations in Kyiv have been hit by jet-powered drones in a wave of targeted Russian attacks as the bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters a new phase of intensity.

At least two people were killed and 12 injured in strikes on two petrol stations on Friday morning, according to the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko.

The rush-hour strikes follow a similar attack on a petrol station on Thursday, the first of its kind in the capital.

At the Ukrnafta petrol station in the Pochaina neighbourhood in northern Kyiv, bystanders said three people had been injured in Friday’s blast – the manager of a nearby car wash, his wife and the driver of a passing car. The blown-out vehicle was stranded by the side of the road, its windows shattered and seats spattered in blood.

Witnesses said they had heard two explosions, and local authorities later said Russia had carried out a double-tap attack on the facility.

Pochaina petrol station. All three strikes targeted sites operated by Ukrnafta Photograph: Amy Hawkins

“This is probably one of the most difficult periods of the war because life is just like on a rollercoaster,” said Anastasiia Demchenko, 30, who works at a delivery company opposite the petrol station. “It feels like life is on the edge.”

All three strikes targeted petrol stations operated by Ukrnafta, a state-owned oil and natural gas extraction company.

Sergiy Fedorenko, the acting head of Naftogaz, Ukrnafta’s parent company, said: “There is, and can be, no military objective behind such attacks. This is terror directed at the civilian population, at peaceful people.”

A list of 18 petrol stations in Kyiv expected to be hit by Russian drones started circulating on Telegram on Wednesday. The three struck so far were on the list.

At the other station hit on Friday, in Desnianskyi district, one of the most densely populated parts of the capital, the manager of a nearby car wash said it had been a miracle that no one had died in the blast.

Fedir Lesovin said the air-raid siren had given the petrol station workers time to run to a nearby shelter, and that a customer waiting outside his business saw the incoming drone and also ran to safety.

Desnianskyi district petrol station was also hit, in one of the most densely populated areas of Kyiv. Photograph: Amy Hawkins

Russia has increased its attacks on Ukrainian petrol stations in recent months. Facilities in the east and south of the country have been repeatedly targeted, but this week’s attacks mark the first time that strikes against a vital part of daily life have been brought to the capital.

Ukraine has also targeted Russian oil infrastructure. Its special forces said this week that they had struck facilities at the Caspian Sea port of Makhachkala.

Kyiv has been pounded by daily drone and missile strikes since late August, at a time when Ukraine is running low on Patriot interceptors. A brief reprieve for the visit of the US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff over the weekend ended on Monday.

The petrol station attacks happened as Volodymyr Zelenskyy was on an overseas trip intended to drum up international support and aid before what is expected to be a difficult winter. On Thursday the Ukrainian president met Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, who offered support to help boost Ukraine’s drone stocks.

title: Trump and Hegseth use 9/11 memorial remarks at Pentagon to defend war on Iran
author: Shrai Popat and Joseph Gedeon in Washington
preview: President and defense secretary try to link worst terrorist attack in US history to current unpopular war US politics live – latest updates Donald Trump and Pete Hegseth used remarks at the memorial ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of 9/11 to defend the US-Israel war on Iran – and suggest the controversial conflict was part of the legacy of the worst terrorist attack in US history.
full_text_clean:
Donald Trump and Pete Hegseth during a 9/11 observance ceremony on the 25th anniversary of the attack on the Pentagon in Washington DC. Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/Reuters

Trump and Hegseth use 9/11 memorial remarks at Pentagon to defend war on Iran

President and defense secretary try to link worst terrorist attack in US history to current unpopular war

Donald Trump and Pete Hegseth used remarks at the memorial ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of 9/11 to defend the US-Israel war on Iran – and suggest the controversial conflict was part of the legacy of the worst terrorist attack in US history.

While such ceremonies on September 11 typically focus on the victims of the 2001 attacks, the US president and his defense secretary each pointed to the war they launched on Iran more than six months ago, with no end in sight.

“We salute every member of the United States military who served in the ‘war on terror’,” Trump said at the Pentagon, which was struck by a hijacked airliner, killing all 64 people onboard and 125 inside the building. “And we salute the service members working right now to ensure the world’s number one sponsor of terror, the Islamic Republic of Iran, will never ever have a nuclear weapon.”

The US president’s decision to stay in Washington has drawn criticism, while his vice‑president, JD Vance, traveled to New York for a memorial at Ground Zero, the site of the World Trade Center’s destruction on 9/11.

Closing out his speech, Trump also tried to draw a direct link between his war on Iran – which is vastly unpopular in the US, according to opinion polls – and the 9/11 terror attacks.

“Today we renew the sacred oath that we first swore in their names a quarter of a century ago. We will never, ever forget,” he said. “That’s why we fight today. We don’t have a choice. There can only be victory. We fight hard. We fight to win.”

Earlier, Hegseth, the US defense secretary, delivered a bellicose speech at the somber memorial. Noting that the Iran war was part of the fight against an “Islamic theocracy that has wished us death for nearly half a century”, he claimed that Iran’s defenses “are gone”, despite evidence to the contrary.

“We’re still sending terrorists where they belong – to hell,” declared Hegseth. “And tankers to the bottom of the ocean where they belong, and we are ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon. The economic pressure tightens every day.”

Hegseth said at the ceremony: “The struggle against evil continued, and it continues now. It will continue until judgment day. Our only answer here on Earth is eternal vigilance.”

He also claimed the threat extended into US borders, warning that “enemies plot to curb our power and kill our citizens, including from Islamic terrorists abroad and at home”.

Hegseth went on to credit Trump with dismantling Iran’s military capabilities, and closed by calling for a new generation of “strong, brave warriors who will say when it matters most, ‘send me’”.

Separately, during the New York City ceremony, the leader of one group of 9/11 victims’ families pleaded with the Trump administration to hold Saudi Arabia accountable for its alleged support of the terrorists who carried out the attacks.

“It has been one betrayal after another. President Trump can still change that,” said Terry Strada, a widow of one of the victims. “Tell the Saudis to stop lying. Tell them that if they want to be friends with the USA, they cannot continue to deny all of this – all of the pain, all of the destruction that we have all been suffering through.”
