title: Iran’s Houthi allies capture strategic island on vital oil shipping route
author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
preview: Rampant Yemeni fighters take control of island in narrow point of Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi is relying on for oil exports Why the rapid Houthi advance matters and what’s at stake Yemen’s rampant Houthi forces have captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the ​world’s vital shipping routes.
full_text_clean:
Houthi fighters on a march to mobilise more fighters against Saudi-backed government troops, in Sana'a on Thursday. Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA

Iran’s Houthi allies capture strategic island on vital oil shipping route

Rampant Yemeni fighters take control of island in narrow point of Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi is relying on for oil exports

Yemen’s rampant Houthi forces have captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the ​world’s vital shipping routes.

The Iran-aligned Houthis took control of the volcanic island after forces allied to the UN-backed, Aden-based government left in the latest of a dramatic series of reverses along Yemen’s west coast in recent days, including the loss of the port city of Mocha on Thursday.

Saudi Arabia, which supports and bankrolls the official Yemen government, mounted air raids on Houthi positions in Mocha on Friday.

The Bab al-Mandab strait links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez canal. Perim island, also known as Mayun, divides the waterway in two, close to its narrowest point. The United Arab Emirates, a former Saudi ally in the anti-Houthi coalition, had been building an airbase on the island before ending its active involvement in the conflict in January.

Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab to export its crude since Iran has been targeting vessels in the strait of Hormuz. About 12% of the world’s goods are typically shipped through the strait.

Full Houthi control of shipping in the strait, alongside Iranian control of the strait of Hormuz, would strengthen the chokeholds of anti-western forces over global energy shipments. Oil prices have risen to more than $100 a barrel as the fighting in Yemen has escalated.

Iran hailed the Houthi advances in an official statement on Friday, its first extended comment on the renewed fighting inside Yemen. Iran and the Houthis have been allied since the Houthis rose to power inside Yemen in 2014.

Fighters loyal to the Houthis march during a rally to recruit more fighters, in Sana’a on Thursday. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

In a statement the Houthis hailed the expulsion of “Saudi enemy” troops from six districts in the Taiz and Hodeidah regions, the capture of 4,500 sq miles, the targeting of “seven military divisions of the Saudi enemy’s forces” and the “killing, capture, and wounding” of hundreds of soldiers. It also claimed to have released hundreds of prisoners “held by the Saudi enemy’s mercenaries for years”.

British diplomatic sources said they did not at present expect Donald Trump to sanction any US bombing of Houthi positions in Yemen, despite requests to do so from Saudi Arabia. The pace of the Houthi advance, and political divisions in the Yemen governorates not controlled by the Houthis, have left western capitals fearful that even the Yemen government capital, Aden, could fall to the Houthis. The UK effectively treated Yemen as a British protectorate until 1967.

The Houthi offensive has cost more than 500 lives and displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Friday.

Perim island seen in a 2021 satellite photograph. Photograph: Planet Labs Inc./AP

The Houthi progress down the Red Sea coast from the port of Hodeidah also strengthens Iran’s hand in trying to reach an agreement with other Gulf states on future control of the strait of Hormuz, the central dispute between the US and Iran. Iran has reached an agreement on temporary approved routes with Oman, the country sharing the southern coast of the Hormuz strait. The proposed deal is supposed to be discussed at a meeting of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) foreign ministers in the Omani coastal city of Salalah on Monday.

The deal, including a temporary approved route for shipping largely under Iranian control, would – if agreed by the GCC – put pressure on the US to lift its highly effective blockade of Iranian oil ports, which is severely damaging the Iranian economy.

The US struck a surprise ceasefire deal with the Houthis in May 2025 after the cost of a bombing campaign escalated, and Houthis gave private assurances that they would not attack US shipping in the Red Sea. The Houthi leadership this week continued to give similar assurances to all shipping except Saudi Arabian oil tankers.

On 14 August Saudi Arabia assembled a 14-country international maritime naval coalition to protect freedom of navigation in the Bab al-Mandab strait and the Gulf of Aden. The coalition, including Bahrain, Pakistan, Somalia, Djibouti, Turkey and Egypt, has so far been invisible, though Riyadh would argue that such a coalition of the willing takes time to assemble.

Recriminations are under way over the fall of Mocha, with the role of Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, the leader of the National Resistance Forces that retreated from the city, under scrutiny. He said the retreat was necessary to regroup his forces.

A view of the Bab al-Mandab strait from the Yemeni coast. Photograph: Khaled Ziad/AFP/Getty Images

On her Facebook page, the Yemeni 2011 Nobel peace prize winner, Tawakkol Karman, called on Yemen’s president, Rashad al-Alimi, to dismiss Saleh and to refer him for investigation and trial on charges of conspiracy and high treason.

Amr al-Bidh, the foreign affairs representative of the separatist political organisation the Southern Transitional Council (STC), said he had warned western diplomats repeatedly of the need for a comprehensive national regional and international strategy to defeat the Houthis, adding occasional airstrikes were not enough.

He accused the Saudis of strategic incompetence and of alienating the southern forces most needed to combat the Houthis.

“The position is now very serious,” he said. “The Houthis’ presence in the strait means they will be able to control the waterways without needing to use sophisticated weapons that as a result they can now use elsewhere. The advance is also likely to give them a new income through control of ports along the west coast of the Red Sea.” The Houthis are already offering concessionary rates to draw traffic from ports controlled by the Yemeni government in the Gulf of Aden.

The STC was the dominant political and military force in southern Yemen until this January, when Saudi Arabia bombed its troops, closed its political organisation down and detained as many as 20 of its leaders in Riyadh.

A Saudi promise of a dialogue about the southern question made in January has never been kept, al-Bidh said, adding that Human Rights Watch warned in a March report that some pro-STC protests in Aden were being repressed with undue violence.

“The betrayal of promises had left the southern population unwilling to leave their home territories to fight the Houthis in the north,” he said. “The Saudis for 10 years have been dependent on the people of the south to deter the Houthis, and the STC with as many as 80,000 troops at its disposal, has been the backbone of that force.”

Saudi Arabia is facing a familiar dilemma: whether to reach a negotiated settlement with the Houthis on the future of Yemen or to try to push the highly stretched Houthi forces back.

Although the Houthis operate independently of Tehran’s instructions, it is hugely to Iran’s advantage for them to be fighting Saudi Arabia, as the Saudis are more likely in turn to put pressure on Washington to relent over Iran.

There is also concern in western capitals about the use of western weaponry by the Saudis in Yemen, and whether their activity complies with international humanitarian law, including whether the Saudi strikes can truly be seen as acts of self-defence.

In a statement the Houthis hailed the expulsion of “Saudi enemy” troops from six districts in the Taiz and Hodeidah regions, the capture of 4,500 sq miles, the targeting of “seven military divisions of the Saudi enemy’s forces” and the “killing, capture, and wounding” of hundreds of soldiers. It also claimed to have released hundreds of prisoners “held by the Saudi enemy’s mercenaries for years”.

British diplomatic sources said they did not at present expect Donald Trump to sanction any US bombing of Houthi positions in Yemen, despite requests to do so from Saudi Arabia. The pace of the Houthi advance, and political divisions in the Yemen governorates not controlled by the Houthis, have left western capitals fearful that even the Yemen government capital, Aden, could fall to the Houthis. The UK effectively treated Yemen as a British protectorate until 1967.

The Houthi offensive has cost more than 500 lives and displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Friday.

Perim island seen in a 2021 satellite photograph. Photograph: Planet Labs Inc./AP

The Houthi progress down the Red Sea coast from the port of Hodeidah also strengthens Iran’s hand in trying to reach an agreement with other Gulf states on future control of the strait of Hormuz, the central dispute between the US and Iran. Iran has reached an agreement on temporary approved routes with Oman, the country sharing the southern coast of the Hormuz strait. The proposed deal is supposed to be discussed at a meeting of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) foreign ministers in the Omani coastal city of Salalah on Monday.

The deal, including a temporary approved route for shipping largely under Iranian control, would – if agreed by the GCC – put pressure on the US to lift its highly effective blockade of Iranian oil ports, which is severely damaging the Iranian economy.

The US struck a surprise ceasefire deal with the Houthis in May 2025 after the cost of a bombing campaign escalated, and Houthis gave private assurances that they would not attack US shipping in the Red Sea. The Houthi leadership this week continued to give similar assurances to all shipping except Saudi Arabian oil tankers.

On 14 August Saudi Arabia assembled a 14-country international maritime naval coalition to protect freedom of navigation in the Bab al-Mandab strait and the Gulf of Aden. The coalition, including Bahrain, Pakistan, Somalia, Djibouti, Turkey and Egypt, has so far been invisible, though Riyadh would argue that such a coalition of the willing takes time to assemble.

Recriminations are under way over the fall of Mocha, with the role of Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, the leader of the National Resistance Forces that retreated from the city, under scrutiny. He said the retreat was necessary to regroup his forces.

A view of the Bab al-Mandab strait from the Yemeni coast. Photograph: Khaled Ziad/AFP/Getty Images

On her Facebook page, the Yemeni 2011 Nobel peace prize winner, Tawakkol Karman, called on Yemen’s president, Rashad al-Alimi, to dismiss Saleh and to refer him for investigation and trial on charges of conspiracy and high treason.

Amr al-Bidh, the foreign affairs representative of the separatist political organisation the Southern Transitional Council (STC), said he had warned western diplomats repeatedly of the need for a comprehensive national regional and international strategy to defeat the Houthis, adding occasional airstrikes were not enough.

He accused the Saudis of strategic incompetence and of alienating the southern forces most needed to combat the Houthis.

“The position is now very serious,” he said. “The Houthis’ presence in the strait means they will be able to control the waterways without needing to use sophisticated weapons that as a result they can now use elsewhere. The advance is also likely to give them a new income through control of ports along the west coast of the Red Sea.” The Houthis are already offering concessionary rates to draw traffic from ports controlled by the Yemeni government in the Gulf of Aden.

The STC was the dominant political and military force in southern Yemen until this January, when Saudi Arabia bombed its troops, closed its political organisation down and detained as many as 20 of its leaders in Riyadh.

A Saudi promise of a dialogue about the southern question made in January has never been kept, al-Bidh said, adding that Human Rights Watch warned in a March report that some pro-STC protests in Aden were being repressed with undue violence.

“The betrayal of promises had left the southern population unwilling to leave their home territories to fight the Houthis in the north,” he said. “The Saudis for 10 years have been dependent on the people of the south to deter the Houthis, and the STC with as many as 80,000 troops at its disposal, has been the backbone of that force.”

Saudi Arabia is facing a familiar dilemma: whether to reach a negotiated settlement with the Houthis on the future of Yemen or to try to push the highly stretched Houthi forces back.

Although the Houthis operate independently of Tehran’s instructions, it is hugely to Iran’s advantage for them to be fighting Saudi Arabia, as the Saudis are more likely in turn to put pressure on Washington to relent over Iran.

There is also concern in western capitals about the use of western weaponry by the Saudis in Yemen, and whether their activity complies with international humanitarian law, including whether the Saudi strikes can truly be seen as acts of self-defence.

author: Emma Graham-Harrison in Jerusalem and Xan Brooks in Venice

full_text_clean:
A scene from NAZA, a documentary produced by the Guardian and directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. Photograph: The Guardian

Secret systems used by Israel in mass killings of Gaza civilians revealed in new film

Testimony from Israeli military insiders involved in surveillance and remote killings features in documentary produced by the Guardian

Testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders ​on the secret ​systems used in ​the war on Gaza​ has been revealed in a new documentary film about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians.

NAZA, a film from the Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, was shown at the Venice international film festival on Thursday as the only documentary competing for its prestigious Golden Lion award.

The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to civilians expected to be killed in a military attack. Produced by the Guardian, it features extensive testimony from Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers involved in the surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians.

Interviews were filmed at night on rooftops in Tel Aviv, on the condition of anonymity because of the risks involved in speaking publicly about Israel’s war activities. The appearance and voices of participants in the film were digitally altered to disguise their identities.

The interviewees detail the secret methods used by the Israeli military in Gaza, including AI-based systems built to identify large numbers of potential low-ranking Hamas targets, who were then bombed in their homes at night, in the knowledge attacks would also kill their families.

Israeli soldiers at a military position overlooking the so-called yellow line in Gaza in May. Photograph: Ariel Schalit/AP

The Israeli military hacked into phones to identify the location of such targets, and covertly listened into conversations with their wives and children moments before they were all killed.

The film also features first-person accounts about the destruction of neighbourhoods where the Israeli military estimated that up to 25% of residents were still sheltering in their homes, the systematic burning of civilian homes, and the killing of civilians at a food distribution site.

Abraham said at a press conference in Venice on Thursday: “We just told these officers: ‘Please describe to us what you did. How do these systems work? Sketch it out for us.’ Sometimes, in just asking the questions, you get the answers.

“Some of them did not express remorse and some did. Some spoke out of indifference, some out of pride.”

The film’s directors, Rachel Szor and Yuval Abhram (centre), with producers and crew members at the Venice film festival on Thursday. Photograph: Yves Herman/Reuters

Several interviewees worked in a secret intelligence unit that reports directly to the office of Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu; one said their mission was to “thwart peace”.

“We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israeli film-makers and journalists to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible,” Abraham and Szor said in their directors’ statement.

The directors stressed the film’s focus was not on “sporadic war crimes committed by rogue soldiers”. “It is on the orders themselves, the policies, the accepted practices, the language and logic that make those practices possible, and the people who operate within them,” they said. “The system and its cogs.”

An explosion after an Israeli airstrike in Gaza City on Wednesday. Photograph: Jehad Alshrafi/AP

The documentary was co-produced by James Wilson and executive produced by Jonathan Glazer, the same team behind the Oscar-winning film The Zone of Interest.

The film received a nearly 25-minute standing ovation after its screening, according to Variety, which called it a record for length of applause not just at Venice but at any major film festival and reported that Glazer embraced Abraham and Szor as it went on, while some members of the audience held up Palestinian flags.

NAZA builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. It was filmed and produced under tight security because of the risk to confidential journalistic sources, and its contents have remained a closely guarded secret before Thursday’s premiere.

Paul Lewis, the Guardian’s head of investigations and an executive producer on the film, described NAZA as the culmination of “years of painstaking work to uncover and verify the systems used by Israeli military intelligence in Gaza”.

Abraham said making the documentary had provided space to explore the collective impact of that work. “In this film we’re talking to 24 people. We are looking at systems of mass killing. There is something about cinema that allows you to explore structures and systems and how you put things together.”

Before the premiere, Alberto Barbera, the Venice film festival’s artistic director, told journalists NAZA would be “truly groundbreaking”, calling it “a politically disruptive and cinematically extremely interesting work”.

“It’s not just any collection of interviews,” Italy’s Cinecittà News quoted Barbera as saying. “It took them three years to convince these Israeli intelligence and military officials to share the work they did when the invasion of Gaza began, and I assure you, their testimonies are shocking.”

Israeli attacks in Gaza since 2023 have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, and injured more than 174,000 others, together representing more than 10% of Gaza’s prewar population.

Israeli restrictions on food shipments created a man-made famine last summer, and the Israeli military razed or damaged more than three-quarters of homes, so surviving Palestinians are now crowded into tent camps with little access to clean water or sanitation.

Israel launched its war after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, when more than 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken to Gaza by militants. The majority of the dead and hostages were civilians.

Abraham and Szor were two of the four co-directors of No Other Land, which won the Oscar for best documentary in 2025.

Drawing a connection between the two films, the directors said: “In the film No Other Land, we spent five years, together with [Palestinian co-directors] Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, documenting the army destroying Palestinian homes in order to paint a larger picture of a system of occupation and ethnic supremacy aimed at the removal of Palestinians from the West Bank.

“In NAZA, we are similarly connecting the dots of a system, gathering the testimonies of two dozen intelligence officers and soldiers and depicting the military systems used to perpetrate what a UN commission and the world’s leading human rights groups have described as a genocide.”

title: Houthis seize key Yemeni port of Mocha in drive to take control of Red Sea coast
author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
preview: Iran and its proxies move closer to full control of two shipping chokepoints as regional conflict widens Explained: why the fighting in Yemen matters globally Houthi forces in Yemen are making a concerted drive to take over the country’s Red Sea coast fully, claiming control of the key port of Mocha in the most serious wave of fighting with the Saudi-backed government in years, bringing the...
full_text_clean:
Fighters loyal to the Houthis take part in a recruitment drive in Sana’a on Thursday. Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty Images

Houthis seize key Yemeni port of Mocha in drive to take control of Red Sea coast

Iran and its proxies move closer to full control of two shipping chokepoints as regional conflict widens

Houthi forces in Yemen are making a concerted drive to take over the country’s Red Sea coast fully, claiming control of the key port of Mocha in the most serious wave of fighting with the Saudi-backed government in years, bringing the Iran-aligned group closer to full control of a key shipping route.

Seizure of the coast and some of the islands in the sea would be a strategic disaster for Saudi Arabia and the US, taking Iran and its proxies closer to full control of two choke points for western shipping on opposite sides of the Arabian peninsula: the Bab al-Mandab at the southern end of the Red Sea and the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

Observers have said a reduction in hostilities – the most intense since the UN-sponsored ceasefire of April 2022 put an end to major military exchanges – now seems unlikely in what is seen as an attempt by the Houthis to open a second front in the Iran-US war, alongside the battle for control of Hormuz.

Baraa Shiban, the Royal United Services Institute’s (Rusi) Yemen specialist, a London-based security thinktank, said the situation in the country was spiralling out of control, adding that the UN-recognised Yemeni government was opening new fronts against the Houthis in the hope of putting more pressure on their forces than they could withstand. But in the past 48 hours the Houthis had major advances south, down Yemen’s west coast, taking them closer to the high ground overlooking the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait.

A screen grab from video footage released by Saudi-backed forces shows a rocket being fired during fighting in Taiz province. Photograph: Yemen National Resistance Forces/AFP/Getty Images

The fighting has also raised questions about whether Saudi Arabia, which on Thursday launched as many as 40 airstrikes on Houthi targets, will activate the Mecca defence agreement and ask its co-signatories, Pakistan and Turkey, to send forces. The pact is designed to be defensive in nature and believed unlikely to apply to Saudi military activities in Yemen.

By taking control of more of the Red Sea coast south of the port of Hodeidah, the Houthis’ aim is to use a new lever to put pressure on Saudi Arabia and the US to agree a deal that lifts the US blockade on Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf. Donald Trump on Wednesday acknowledged he did not expect the war with Iran to end before the US midterm elections at the start of November.

The latest phase in the escalation began when Houthis attacked energy installations and southern cities in Saudi Arabia using drones and ballistic missiles. In response, the kingdom’s military forces launched at least 15 strikes between 3 and 7 September.

The aftermath of Houthi strikes on Mocha last month. The rebel group claims it now controls the port. Photograph: Al Joumhouriya TV/Reuters

The conflict data monitor Acled estimated there were 276 fatalities over the five-day period alone. The fighting has continued, with the Houthis claiming control of Mocha in Taiz province, as well as the inland city of Hays and the Khalid ibn al-Walid camp, the largest military base in the region. One Houthi-linked estimate suggested its forces had gained control of more than 2,320 sq miles (6,000 sq km) of land.

The commander of the Yemeni government forces, Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, admitted he had organised a strategic retreat south of Mocha in order to regroup in a secure location. “The armed forces in the western coast paid a heavy price – martyrs and wounded – over the past days as they confronted the Houthi attack planned by Iran, and supported by it,” he said. Analysts claimed that the effectiveness of Yemen’s government forces was weakened by internal divisions, as well as external pressure from Saudi Arabia.

A satellite image shows smoke billowing from an Aramco oil depot near the Saudi city of Abha after a Houthi attack. Photograph: Planet Labs/AFP/Getty Images

The latter, meanwhile, continues to take advantage of its air superiority to attack Houthi positions, though government sources acknowledged Houthi ground advances along the coast and their missile strikes on the strategic Red Sea islands of Zuqar and Hanish.

The clashes have raged across Yemen, including Ad Dali, al-Bayda, Marib, Shabwah, al-Jawf, Hodeidah, and Taiz. In the initial days of the renewed conflict the Houthis were forced back in some areas as battles on multiple fronts overstretched their resources and fighter numbers.

The Houthis will be hoping political divisions inside the Yemeni government, reflected in a lack of an integrated military, will slowly give them the upper hand. The United Arab Emirates, previously a powerful player in southern Yemen where it backed the separatist forces of the Southern Transitional Council, withdrew its financial and military support at the turn of the year. The southern forces have refused to fight outside their own region.

A screen grab from video footage released by the Saudi-backed forces shows a fighter firing at Houthi forces in Taiz province. Photograph: Yemen National Resistance Forces/AFP/Getty Images

“ A reduction in hostilities anytime soon seems unlikely, as both sides continue to escalate with the goal of inflicting enough damage to the other side to force a compromise,” said Sherwan Hindreen Ali, a Yemen analyst for Acled. “In terms of military capability, both sides are more equal compared to the immediate period prior to the 2022 ceasefire when the Houthis had the upper hand.”

He added: “Fighting will remain focused on the fronts of the Red Sea coast in Hodeidah and Taiz, where both the Houthis and the Saudi Arabia-Yemen government have a vested interest in claiming the whole territory to deprive the other side of effective control of the strait of Bab al-Mandab.”

The head of the Houthis’ national delegating negotiating team, Muhammad Abdul Salam, insisted non-Saudi commercial shipping would not be attacked.

The fighting has contributed to the price of oil rising above $100 a barrel after weeks when it was trading closer to $80.

Footage reportedly shows Houthi attacks on Saudi-backed forces in al-Jawf province. Photograph: Ansarullah Media Centre/AFP/Getty Images

The escalation to this week’s all-out violence has been a slow process. It began after a senior delegation of the Houthi group, which has long been in a complex alliance with Iran, flew to Tehran for the funeral of the Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei in July, returning in an Iranian plane that the Saudis refused to land in rebel-controlled Sana’a.

The Saudis instead bombed the runway, leading the Houthis to announce a Red Sea naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in what the Yemeni group described as a blockade for a blockade. The 20 July announcement of the blockade was followed by a strike on Saudi Arabia’s Jazan refinery on 25 July and on a tanker off Yanbu on 24 August.

Saudi Arabia has become reliant on the Red Sea route for trade after Iran throttled shipping through the strait of Hormuz as a result of US-Israeli attacks.

title: Tens of millions of people fail to get humanitarian aid as global system crumbles
author: Kaamil Ahmed
preview: Funding cuts in 2025 left women, children, older and displaced people hard hit, with 64m fewer people receiving aid The humanitarian aid system is crumbling as funding shrinks, pressures increase and governments not only fail to protect civilians but are increasingly responsible for endangering them, a new report warned on Thursday as figures revealed 64 million fewer people received aid last...
full_text_clean:
People queue for food during a severe drought in Kenya’s Turkana county in February. Global aid contributions fell by 30% between 2022 and 2025. Photograph: Patrick Ngugi/AP

Tens of millions of people fail to get humanitarian aid as global system crumbles

Funding cuts in 2025 left women, children, older and displaced people hard hit, with 64m fewer people receiving aid

The humanitarian aid system is crumbling as funding shrinks, pressures increase and governments not only fail to protect civilians but are increasingly responsible for endangering them, a new report warned on Thursday as figures revealed 64 million fewer people received aid last year.

With aid contributions cut by 30% between 2022 and 2025 and thousands of aid workers losing their jobs, the humanitarian system has suffered one of its biggest contractions since being formed in the post-second world war era, according to the State of the Humanitarian System 2026 report.

In 2025, only those whose lives were in immediate danger became the focus, while support for longer-term issues and the ability to recover from crises was drastically scaled back.

Jennifer Doherty, co-author of the report produced by the humanitarian organisation Active Learning Network for Accountability and Performance (Alnap), said: “The impacts were not felt equally. The combination of reduced funding and restrictive politics meant women, children, elderly people and displaced people were especially hardest hit.”

Doherty, who said up to 23% of humanitarian staffing was estimated to have been lost in 2025, said: “Specialised services closed and targeted support became harder to sustain.”

According to the report, funding fell to an estimated $33.3bn (£24.6bn) in 2025, from a peak of $47.5bn in 2022.

While USAID sustained the most dramatic cuts, with a 55% reduction in 2025, there were also cuts by other leading donors, with 13 of the top 20 reducing their aid donations last year.

The report also highlighted the growing pressure from governments on how aid could be spent, such as the US spending freeze on programmes considered driven by diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policies.

The aid cuts also meant that for the few people who did receive support, the targeted amount for each person dropped from $178 in 2021 to $90 in 2025, despite the actual needs of each person having risen to $255.

An aggravating factor was that governments not only failed in their duties to protect civilians but were also often actually endangering people. States were responsible for 64% of attacks on healthcare workers and largely responsible for violence that affected aid workers through the use of airstrikes.

Displaced people receive food aid in Al-Khawkhah, in Yemen’s Hodeidah province, in July. Photograph: Khaled Ziad/AFP/Getty Images

Yemen was one of the countries badly affected by aid cuts, with nutrition worsening and diphtheria cases rising because vaccination campaigns were suspended.

Mohammed Bahashwan, Action for Humanity’s country director in Yemen, said diminishing levels of aid were exacerbating the crises faced by families.

“Problems are not occurring separately. A family may have lost its income, be unable to afford food, have a malnourished child and still need to travel considerable distances or pay costs they cannot afford to access healthcare,” he said.

The report said there were examples of the humanitarian system mobilising to support those most in need, often led by local aid organisations, and of diaspora networks stepping in. But it also said the international system did not coordinate well with these networks and that it was often local aid organisations and staff who were worst affected by cuts.

Meg Sattler, chief executive of the Vienna-based organisation Ground Truth Solutions, which carries out regular surveys of people who need aid, said there should be more focus on localisation because the international humanitarian system had not adapted fast enough or pushed back against the cuts and stipulations imposed by the US.

“We have definitely spoken to people feeling the pinch of this contraction. It is especially causing distress where aid is now considered ‘life-saving only’ and isn’t letting people do things such as send their kids to school or save to start a business – things that would help them be less reliant on aid in the future,” she said.

title: ‘Our forefathers are coming back’: Naga people celebrate after Oxford museum agrees to return remains
author: Tora Agarwala
preview: Following six years of talks, Pitt Rivers Museum will return body parts collected by British colonial administrators to north-east India Anthropologists and community leaders from Nagaland, a remote state in north-eastern India bordering Myanmar, have expressed joy and relief that human remains belonging to their ancestors that had been on display in a British museum for nearly a century are...
full_text_clean:
The Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford is returning 39 pieces of human remains belonging to the Naga tribes after six years of negotiations. Photograph: Pitt Rivers Museum

‘Our forefathers are coming back’: Naga people celebrate after Oxford museum agrees to return remains

Following six years of talks, Pitt Rivers Museum will return body parts collected by British colonial administrators to north-east India

Anthropologists and community leaders from Nagaland, a remote state in north-eastern India bordering Myanmar, have expressed joy and relief that human remains belonging to their ancestors that had been on display in a British museum for nearly a century are finally being returned.

On Monday, the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford announced that 39 pieces of human remains – including parts of skulls, a finger and a piece of skin with hair – belonging to the Naga tribes, will be returned to Nagaland after six years of negotiation between the community and the museum.

For the Nagas, the repatriation is not just about “bones and ancestral remains … It is about memory returning to where it belongs,” the community said in a statement.

“We are at peace,” said A Peihwang Wangsa, an Indigenous Konyak man involved in the repatriation negotiations. “Our forefathers are coming back.”

Wangsa, whose ancestors’ remains are among those being returned, added that the homecoming would be a moment of “mourning and celebration”.

NT Thamlong Phom, a Naga community leader from the Phom sub-tribe, said: “I feel joy, I feel blessed.

“Ever since the announcement was made, my entire community has felt happy,” he said. “Our ancestors’ spirit will have a final resting place.”

Thejao Vihienuo, who is also part of the repatriation discussions and went to Oxford in 2025, said he had been “angry and unhappy” to see the remains of his ancestors, which he said had been “taken in a most dubious manner”.

“It was displayed as if it was a trophy, but they silently spoke of the atrocities the British committed on our people,” he said.

The return caused “mixed feelings”, he said, but added: “We owe it to our ancestors to bring their remains back and put them to peaceful rest. And also to our younger generation to decolonise their minds and show that our children are not inferior to any white man.”

The Nagas are a transnational Indigenous group of tribes living in India’s north-east and parts of Myanmar, once associated with headhunting but now predominantly Christian.

The Pitt Rivers Museum, home to one of the world’s largest ethnological collections, has more than 6,500 Naga objects, 898 of which were on display. Most of the collection was “ coercively ” acquired by the colonial administrators James Philip Mills and John Henry Hutton.

Prof Dolly Kikon, a Naga anthropologist (kneeling, centre, in a red scarf) with other Naga delegates and museum staff. Photograph: Pitt Rivers Museum

The human remains were displayed at the museum for 80 years. In 2020, they were put into storage during a revamp aimed at addressing the institution’s colonial past and how exhibiting human remains “reinforced racist and stereotypical thinking” of other cultures.

The museum said in a statement: “Thirty-nine Naga ancestors will soon begin their journey home from Oxford to Nagaland.”

In November, a Naga delegation will visit Oxford for a handover ceremony and the remains are expected to arrive in Nagaland before the end of the year. They will be laid to rest in a traditional community ceremony in the state capital, Kohima.

The repatriation negotiations were led by representatives from all of the Naga tribes.

“It has been a journey of redemption,” said Prof Dolly Kikon, a Naga anthropologist. “This shows that we are no longer victims of colonial violence. We embrace our roles as people who find redemption and healing by giving dignity and honour to a very violent past.”

The negotiations started in 2020, when Kikon wrote to the museum after reading “ an article in the Guardian that they were doing an ethical review” of the collection. “They replied within 24 hours,” said Kikon.

That was just the beginning of a lengthy process that soon expanded into a wider community-led campaign.

The Forum for Naga Reconciliation, a community peace group, assembled a team known as Recover, Restore and Decolonise, bringing together Naga volunteers from across the region to work on the repatriation effort.

Members of the Naga delegation view the relics on display at the Pitt Rivers Museum. Photograph: Pitt Rivers Museum

“They travelled to villages and organised meetings to inform people about the remains,” said Arkotong Longkumer, a Naga anthropologist who worked closely with Kikon to lead the initiative, which he described as “open and transparent”.

“It was an intergenerational journey that brought together students, civil society, tribal leaders and the church,” said Longkumer, who teaches at Edinburgh University.

A Naga delegation, including tribal leaders, visited Oxford in 2025 to officially register a claim to the remains.

“I had never known our ancestral human remains had been taken away like that,” said Wangsa. “I felt angry when I saw them.”

Laura Van Broekhoven, director of the Pitt Rivers Museum and a professor of museum studies and ethics at Oxford University, said the museum was completing paperwork to enable the return of the remains.

“We will then start working towards the ceremonial aspects so we can have everything ready,” she said. “In our experience, handover ceremonies can be very emotional.”

title: ‘Trust deficit’: Why India’s economic data has sparked a furore
author: Niha Masih
preview: India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous – that appears to have eroded • Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here There isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception.
full_text_clean:
Critics say the India government has changed methologies and suppressed findings about its GDP figures. Photograph: Narinder Nanu/AFP/Getty Images

‘Trust deficit’: Why India’s economic data has sparked a furore

India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous – that appears to have eroded

T here isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher than the forecast 7%. It sparked a furore.

Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors. According to Garg, the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%.

The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a more fundamental problem: a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus?

Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings.

In November, the International Monetary Fund rated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data.

Critics say the government has hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure. Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty Images

India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years.

“There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.”

In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019, a Business Standard journalist revealed that the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest. The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only released months later.

Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, was delayed in 2021. Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.)

Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%.

But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism.

The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended.

The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician Pronab Sen have pointed out, is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used.

Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young people have taken to the streets in frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future.

Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke at a protest against leaked exam papers, as young people in India face soaring rates of unemployment. Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images

Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month.

That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.

The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”

What else we’re reading about

Mumbai bound … British singer Olivia Dean is headed to Lollapalooza. Photograph: Isabel Infantes/Reuters

Lollapalooza | British pop star Olivia Dean is to perform in India for the first time in January when she headlines Lollapalooza 2027 in Mumbai. Limp Bizkit is another headline act at the two-day event. Indian artists on the lineup include Ricky Kej (performing with Stewart Copeland) and Aditya Gadhvi.

The price of gold | Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked Indians once again to refrain from buying gold and travelling abroad. He had first made an appeal to self-reliance in May, in part to conserve India’s declining foreign exchange reserves amid a rise in import prices and global energy shocks.

Census 2027 | The new and expanded questionnaire for the 2027 census is raising concerns, reports Scroll’s Anant Gupta. The questionnaire asks respondents for details about their identity documents, as well as their parents’ religion and place of birth. Several of these questions were part of the controversial National Population Register that has remained in abeyance since 2020 and was controversial due to fears that the data might be used to target minorities through a citizenship registry.

Guest shelf

A recommendation from someone with great taste

Bean-to-bar movement … artisanal chocolate is having a moment. Photograph: Manam

Singer Prateek Kuhad (@prateekkuhad), whose latest album, Full Moon Chamber, was released in July, shares an indulgent treat: “I’m a big fan of artisanal Indian chocolate makers. I really like Manam, Carra and Naviluna, and there are many others. Although India has been growing cacao [commercially] since the 1960s, its craft bean-to-bar movement is more recent. Even a plain chocolate bar from one of these makers can be remarkably complex and delicious. More people outside India should know about it and try it.”

Count it

A controversial revision … one-third of the electorate in Delhi have been deleted from voter lists. Photograph: Reuters

One-third of the electorate in Delhi, about 4.76 million voters, have been deleted from the draft voting list as the Election Commission carries out a contentious revision of its rolls across states. So far, about 130 million names have been dropped from draft rolls in 30 states and union territories, the Indian Express reported.

Vibe check

First of many mashups … Ismail Langa Group pose with a larger-than-life image of Shakira. Photograph: Ismail Langa

Earlier this year, Shakira’s concerts in India was postponed. But Rajasthani folk musicians the Ismail Langa Group (@ismaillanga_official) decided the music had to go on, in their own way. Their mashup of the Colombian star’s Hips Don’t Lie with the traditional folk song called Moruda has got everyone grooving (42m views and counting).

It took two months to pull off, says creative director Jagirdar RV. Most artists in the group, aged between 23 and 60, don’t speak or read English and learned the lyrics by rote. The song choice was simple, he said, because it “has a very nice vibe which matched our vibe”.

It’s been a breakout year for the group, which had a semi-final run on India’s Got Talent and are becoming known for taking folk songs to gen Z audiences on Instagram. They are working on their next English mashup – just not spilling which song, yet.

Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month.

That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.

The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”

What else we’re reading about

Mumbai bound … British singer Olivia Dean is headed to Lollapalooza. Photograph: Isabel Infantes/Reuters

Lollapalooza | British pop star Olivia Dean is to perform in India for the first time in January when she headlines Lollapalooza 2027 in Mumbai. Limp Bizkit is another headline act at the two-day event. Indian artists on the lineup include Ricky Kej (performing with Stewart Copeland) and Aditya Gadhvi.

The price of gold | Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked Indians once again to refrain from buying gold and travelling abroad. He had first made an appeal to self-reliance in May, in part to conserve India’s declining foreign exchange reserves amid a rise in import prices and global energy shocks.

Census 2027 | The new and expanded questionnaire for the 2027 census is raising concerns, reports Scroll’s Anant Gupta. The questionnaire asks respondents for details about their identity documents, as well as their parents’ religion and place of birth. Several of these questions were part of the controversial National Population Register that has remained in abeyance since 2020 and was controversial due to fears that the data might be used to target minorities through a citizenship registry.

Guest shelf

A recommendation from someone with great taste

Bean-to-bar movement … artisanal chocolate is having a moment. Photograph: Manam

Singer Prateek Kuhad (@prateekkuhad), whose latest album, Full Moon Chamber, was released in July, shares an indulgent treat: “I’m a big fan of artisanal Indian chocolate makers. I really like Manam, Carra and Naviluna, and there are many others. Although India has been growing cacao [commercially] since the 1960s, its craft bean-to-bar movement is more recent. Even a plain chocolate bar from one of these makers can be remarkably complex and delicious. More people outside India should know about it and try it.”

Count it

A controversial revision … one-third of the electorate in Delhi have been deleted from voter lists. Photograph: Reuters

One-third of the electorate in Delhi, about 4.76 million voters, have been deleted from the draft voting list as the Election Commission carries out a contentious revision of its rolls across states. So far, about 130 million names have been dropped from draft rolls in 30 states and union territories, the Indian Express reported.

Vibe check

First of many mashups … Ismail Langa Group pose with a larger-than-life image of Shakira. Photograph: Ismail Langa

Earlier this year, Shakira’s concerts in India was postponed. But Rajasthani folk musicians the Ismail Langa Group (@ismaillanga_official) decided the music had to go on, in their own way. Their mashup of the Colombian star’s Hips Don’t Lie with the traditional folk song called Moruda has got everyone grooving (42m views and counting).

It took two months to pull off, says creative director Jagirdar RV. Most artists in the group, aged between 23 and 60, don’t speak or read English and learned the lyrics by rote. The song choice was simple, he said, because it “has a very nice vibe which matched our vibe”.

It’s been a breakout year for the group, which had a semi-final run on India’s Got Talent and are becoming known for taking folk songs to gen Z audiences on Instagram. They are working on their next English mashup – just not spilling which song, yet.

author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Kathmandu

full_text_clean:
A woman looks on as heavy machinery works in the aftermath of deadly flash floods and a mudslide near the Nepal-Tibet border. Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/Reuters

Nepal says big polluters must ‘wake up’ as it calls for climate compensation over flood disaster

Foreign minister Shisir Khanal tells the Guardian the world’s biggest economies need to help Nepal, which contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions

Nepal is demanding $20m in climate compensation for the recent devastating floods, as a senior minister called on the world’s most polluting countries to “wake up” and accept shared responsibility for a disaster that led to the death or disappearance of more than 6,000 people.

Scientists believe the climate crisis had a role to play in the floods, which were triggered when a melting glacier partially collapsed and set off a deadly landslide and flash flooding through Chinese-controlled Tibet and Nepal in late August. So far, more than 1,300 are confirmed dead and more than 5,500 still missing, with hopes of their survival diminished after 12 days of rescue operations.

Speaking to the Guardian, Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, was forthright in his call for climate justice and said it was imperative the world’s biggest economies stepped up to help Nepal recover and rebuild after the catastrophic floods.

Nepal contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, while its neighbours India and China are among the world’s biggest emitters. The mountains of the Himalayas – which span across India, China, Nepal and Bhutan – have been warming at a rate nearly 50% faster than the global average.

In 2023, the UN said Nepal’s mountains had lost close to a third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.

Khanal emphasised that the recent disaster was far more extreme than any flooding regularly seen during the monsoon season, and said the magnitude of damage was on par with the 2015 earthquake that left much of the country in ruins.

An excavator repairs a damaged road in Nepal near the Trishuli River on Monday. Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/Reuters

“This felt like a tsunami that was coming from the Himalayas,” he said. “We experienced waves as high as 60, 70 feet, which were mixed with debris, mud, stones, rocks, and came at the speed of almost 180km per hour. Towns, villages and highways were completely wiped out and there are some areas still disconnected.”

Khanal confirmed that Nepal’s ministry of finance and ministry of environment had written a joint letter to the UN’s fund for responding to loss and damage – which was set up in 2022 in line with the Paris climate agreement – to request $20m in climate-related damages.

“We have contributed so little to climate change,” he said. “It is imperative for those in the global community who benefit from larger, much more polluting economies, and whose historical contribution to greenhouse gases is much bigger than ours, to accept a shared responsibility. This affects all of humanity.”

For Nepal, the disaster was particularly worrying because it was “one of the strongest warning signals that we’ve experienced of what’s to come”, he said.

“The global community should not see this as one-off disaster; it should be viewed in the context of the changing climate in the Himalayas,” he said. “We know it is going to be a recurring scenario that more and more communities, not just in Nepal but around the world, will have to face.”

Khanal acknowledged that the compensation amount Nepal has requested from the UN was “obviously not nearly enough to cover the damage that we have sustained”. According to some estimates, the total damage caused by the floods will be upwards of $5bn, though Khanal said it could be even higher.

Upwards of 20,000 homes will probably have to be rebuilt, as well as the main highway. Villages built in vulnerable areas along the river, some of which washed away entirely, may have to be relocated to higher, safer ground.

While Khanal initially singled out India and China as countries that should step in to help – while avoiding mention of the US, which is the world’s biggest polluter – he rowed back on those comments, saying: “It is not just about shifting the blame to one or the other country, it’s about us all working together.”

Damaged buildings on the banks of the Trishuli River. Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/Reuters

He emphasised that the compensation demand was also meant to act as a “wake-up call for the global community to establish a more robust mechanism to help vulnerable and small economies like Nepal”.

The UN has admitted the loss and damage fund is already facing a “significant financing gap”. The fund has already received requests totalling $2.8bn from about 119 countries, but so far only around $400m has been given by the international community. The US has given just $17m, after Donald Trump withdrew from the Paris agreement.

Khanal acknowledged there were “political challenges” in getting Nepal the climate compensation it was demanding.

“Yes there always will be people who may not agree to our perspective or deny there is climate change, but there are also people who deny that the Earth is round,” he said bluntly.

He emphasised the importance of funds being made available not just for immediate disaster response but also for preparedness and mitigation for climate-related risk.

Khanal rebuffed allegations that China had failed to give an adequate warning or share data with Nepal about the impending floods. He said he was in discussion with China about enhancing coordination and data sharing for the Himalayan region.

“With the benefit of hindsight, we can now see that this glacier was fragile and had been receding in the past six months,” he said.

“But before the floods hit, there was no knowledge on our part, or on the part of Chinese scientists, that this particular collapse was imminent. I do not believe any of us had any idea of the threat until it happened.”

title: Rescuers in Nepal find two more people alive after flash flood disaster
author: William Christou
preview: Chinese man at Trishuli hydropower project and Nepali woman in Nuwakot found 10 days into rescue operation Emergency responders have rescued a Chinese man and a Nepali woman in two separate operations as authorities continued to search for thousands of people missing 10 days after massive floods hit Nepal.
full_text_clean:
Rescuers in Nepal find two more people alive after flash flood disaster

Chinese man at Trishuli hydropower project and Nepali woman in Nuwakot found 10 days into rescue operation

Emergency responders have rescued a Chinese man and a Nepali woman in two separate operations as authorities continued to search for thousands of people missing 10 days after massive floods hit Nepal.

The Nepali military said on Saturday a joint team comprising personnel from its army and South Korean disaster experts rescued the man from a 225-metre (740ft) tunnel in the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project, and that he was undergoing a health assessment. Pictures showed him being evacuated by helicopter after being carried out of the tunnel.

Rescue efforts have focused on a dozen hydropower projects across Nepal, where about 900 workers are missing, 500 of whom are thought to be trapped in huge tunnels. International rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the US have been searching through debris and damaged structures at the projects to try to find survivors.

Two Nepali workers were rescued from another tunnel in a hydro-station on the Trishuli River on Friday.

Experts have said the possibility of finding missing people alive in the tunnels is diminishing.

The Nepali woman, 64, was rescued from a damaged house in the devastated town of Nuwakot. Photos published by the Nepali army showed rescuers discovering the woman submerged in mud before she was pulled to safety and airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment. Members of Nepal’s police force cheered as she was pulled from the home, the lower half of which was buried in thick sludge.

Emergency responders have been working to find survivors from the devastating floods in Nepal, which were triggered by a glacial and rock collapse on 26 August. Their work has been complicated by the massive infrastructural damage caused by the floods, with more than 40 bridges having collapsed and rivers swelling unpredictably.

At least 1,375 people have been killed in the floods, with more than 5,000 missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

title: Two workers pulled alive from tunnel nine days after Nepal-Tibet floods
author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Gaurav Pokharel in Kathmandu
preview: Officials say pair were rescued from Trishuli 3A hydropower tunnel in Nepal after being trapped at depth of 170 metres Two people have been pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal nine days after deadly flash floods buried the projects in deep mud and left them trapped.
full_text_clean:
Workers pulled alive from hydropower tunnel nine days after Nepal flood disaster – video

Two workers pulled alive from tunnel nine days after Nepal-Tibet floods

Officials say pair were rescued from Trishuli 3A hydropower tunnel in Nepal after being trapped at depth of 170 metres

Two people have been pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal nine days after deadly flash floods buried the projects in deep mud and left them trapped.

The workers were rescued during an operation at the Trishuli 3A tunnel, a hydropower project in one of the areas worst affected by last week’s floods, according to the army spokesperson Brig Gen Raja Ram Basnet.

Sanjay Shah, a foreman, was the first to be rescued and was taken to the army barracks in Trishuli. Another person, identified as Kabir Maharjan, a project supervisor, was also pulled from the tunnel. They were recovered from a depth of 170 metres (558ft) inside the tunnel, Basnet said.

A senior police official confirmed that a body had also been found during the rescue operation, which has yet to be identified. By Friday afternoon, police confirmed they had halted the search as they had found no more signs of life.

Nepal’s army released images of Shah being pulled from the small dark entrance of a tunnel. He emerged covered in mud but conscious and was carried from the site on a rescuer’s shoulder.

Speaking to army officials after he was rescued, Shah’s first question was: “What day is it?”

Shah said he had been in the tunnel’s control room at the time of the flood, alongside about 40 to 45 others. “Since I was in the control room, my responsibility was to save everyone’s lives,” he said. “After such an accident, I couldn’t just run away by myself. I had to save everyone.”

A survivor is carried out after being rescued from inside the tunnel. Photograph: Nepal Army/Reuters

He said that after realising there had been a major accident, he raced through the tunnel telling people to run and save themselves. “In doing so, I lost time. In the end, I couldn’t get out myself,” he said.

To keep himself calm in the darkness of the tunnel, Shah said he spent his time chanting mantras. He said that while trapped, he had heard the voices of three or four others.

“We were communicating by shouting to each other from nearby. There could also be people inside the powerhouse. Some of them may not have been able to escape,” he said.

Officials said the two men had been flown to a hospital in Kathmandu. Shah was said to be stable but Maharjan was in a critical condition and had been transferred to intensive care.

Hirashova Maharjan, Kabir’s wife, said he had been in shock at first and was not talking, but had since said “a few words”. She said he had an injury to his leg and was extremely jaundiced.

“He did not even recognise me initially. He only said: ‘Where am I? What happened to me?’ He did not say anything else,” she said. “He is better now. He said he wanted some water, so I gave him water. Then I asked him if he recognised me, and he said yes. He nodded his head.”

“We had almost lost hope,” she said, adding that when she saw the photos of him being pulled from the tunnel, “I was so happy that I cried.”

Hirashova Maharjan, left, with a family member after visiting her husband in hospital in Kathmandu on Friday. Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images

Most of the hydropower projects along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the valley last week, triggered by ‌the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet.

At least 1,287 people were killed in the floods and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on the hydropower tunnels, where authorities believe workers may ⁠have survived for more than a week in air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued across several projects.

Large boulders and flood waters had deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud. At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels.

Speaking over the phone from the rescue site, Amrit Thapa, deputy superintendent of the armed police force, who is part of the seven-person search and rescue team, said they had managed to crawl the length of the tunnel looking for survivors. They were accompanied by a team from the Nepal army.

“The team crawled through areas for about 10 to 15 metres and reached the main section,” said Thapa. “When we went to the final point, we found a body on the remaining upper level.”

Thapa said that “except for two sections, the entire tunnel was filled with debris. After checking everything, we did not hear any further voices. We also searched the entire powerhouse area, but so far, nothing else has been found.”

An aerial view of damage in a village in Rasuwa district following the flash floods. Photograph: Narendra Shrestha/EPA

Army and specialist teams have been working round the clock to try to clear debris from the tunnel entrance. At least 550 workers are missing from the hydropower project along the Trishuli River, according to the Independent Power Producers’ Association of Nepal.

In total, local authorities estimate about 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects high up in the Himalayas, with about 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels.

Rescue efforts have also focused on Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, where Nepali authorities said they were confident that 46 workers trapped in an underground chamber in the plant were still alive.

Thapa said that “except for two sections, the entire tunnel was filled with debris. After checking everything, we did not hear any further voices. We also searched the entire powerhouse area, but so far, nothing else has been found.”

An aerial view of damage in a village in Rasuwa district following the flash floods. Photograph: Narendra Shrestha/EPA

Army and specialist teams have been working round the clock to try to clear debris from the tunnel entrance. At least 550 workers are missing from the hydropower project along the Trishuli River, according to the Independent Power Producers’ Association of Nepal.

In total, local authorities estimate about 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects high up in the Himalayas, with about 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels.

Rescue efforts have also focused on Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, where Nepali authorities said they were confident that 46 workers trapped in an underground chamber in the plant were still alive.

title: Man sacked by Grand Theft Auto maker believes employees were put on ‘watch list’
author: Patrick Greenfield
preview: UK employment tribunal examines whether Rockstar Games unlawfully fired 31 staff for trade union activity A worker fired by the makers of Grand Theft Auto has said he believed employees were put on a “watch list” after signing a petition about remote working.
full_text_clean:
Dayne Oram takes part in a rally outside the Rockstar Games tribunal in Glasgow. Photograph: Jane Barlow/PA

Man sacked by Grand Theft Auto maker believes employees were put on ‘watch list’

UK employment tribunal examines whether Rockstar Games unlawfully fired 31 staff for trade union activity

A worker fired by the makers of Grand Theft Auto has said he believed employees were put on a “watch list” after signing a petition about remote working.

Dayne Oram told an employment tribunal in Glasgow examining whether Rockstar Games unlawfully fired 31 employees for trade union activity on Friday that he thought the company started keeping an eye on a group of workers after the petition was sent to leadership in 2023.

Rockstar, which disputes the claims, says Oram and his colleagues were dismissed for gross misconduct after confidential company information was shared, not because of trade union membership or activity.

The workers had been helping to make Grand Theft Auto VI, which is set for release on 19 November and will probably be among the biggest launches in gaming history. The production for the game, which has reportedly generated more than $3bn (£2.27bn) in preorders, is led from the company’s Edinburgh office Rockstar North.

Grand Theft Auto 6 is set for release in November. Illustration: Rockstar Games

Much of the case relies on what was shared in a Discord forum, used by about 300 Rockstar employees to discuss the company. Oram was involved in setting up the forum and helped moderate it, which is where Rockstar says sensitive information was shared and discussed.

Oram told the tribunal that discussions on the forum could “get a bit out of hand”. Thomas Cordrey, representing Rockstar at the tribunal, read Oram the forum rules requiring workers to remain “professional and constructive” when posting. Cordrey suggested that the rules had been “routinely broken”.

Cordrey read out a number of Discord posts where he suggested employees were making disparaging remarks about the company and management, including messages in which one was called “cowardly corporate fucks” and another was called a “cunt”.

Oram told the tribunal that he would probably “remake” some of the moderation decisions if he had the chance to do so again, but said moderators did not want to “over-police” the channel.

Oram also said he believed there was a connection between the list of names who signed the 2023 petition about remote working and the eventual firings in 2025. But Cordrey questioned whether this was really the case when 141 of 154 people who signed it were not fired.

Rockstar Games’ Edinburgh office. Photograph: Jane Barlow/PA

“It was maybe the start of them keeping an eye on things,” Oram told the tribunal.

The case is expected to last about six weeks, with testimony from Rockstar Games witnesses set for October. The company remains in talks with current workers, who hope official union recognition can be secured before the release of GTA VI.

In total, 34 Rockstar workers were fired last year, including three in Canada who are not taking part in the tribunal. Of the 31 who were based in Scotland, 23 are involved in the case and are being represented by the Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain.

A spokesperson for Rockstar Games said: “Rockstar Games’ position has been clear and consistent throughout.

“Individuals across the UK and Canada were dismissed for gross misconduct following the sharing of confidential company information, not because of alleged trade union membership or activity. We reject the claims and will defend them vigorously before the tribunal,” the said.

The tribunal in Glasgow continues before the judge Lucy Wiseman.

title: Northern Ireland schools must give girls option to wear trousers from next year
author: Rory Carroll Ireland correspondent
preview: DUP education minister accused of dragging feet before revising guidelines on uniform Schools in Northern Ireland must give girls the choice to wear trousers as part of their uniforms as well as for PE and games, according to revised guidelines.
full_text_clean:
A law passed last year aimed at reducing the cost of uniforms gave girls the legal right to challenge schools that banned them from wearing trousers, but campaigners said it did not got far enough. Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/Alamy

Northern Ireland schools must give girls option to wear trousers from next year

DUP education minister accused of dragging feet before revising guidelines on uniform

Schools in Northern Ireland must give girls the choice to wear trousers as part of their uniforms as well as for PE and games, according to revised guidelines.

From next year schools would no longer be able to prohibit female pupils from wearing trousers, Paul Givan, the country’s education minister, said on Friday. “Today, I am taking that decision, that will be formally communicated, schools will be hearing from me,” he told the BBC.

A law passed last year that was aimed at reducing the cost of uniforms gave girls the legal right to challenge schools that banned them from wearing trousers.

However, campaigners said the change did not go far enough and put pressure on Givan, a Democratic Unionist party member of the Northern Ireland assembly (MLA) who said his own daughters wore skirts to school, to revise the guidelines.

Givan said he had to strike a balance between schools’ autonomy and the level of prescription in departmental guidelines. “I have listened carefully over recent months to young people and the message is clear: girls want the choice to wear trousers as part of their school uniform.”

The revised guidelines would not go into immediate effect to give schools time to update their policies, said Givan.

Other parties welcomed the change but accused the education minister of dragging his feet.

“I’m glad that it appears the minister has seen fit to U-turn on his decision not to ensure that all girls have the right to wear trousers as part of their school uniform,” said Nick Mathison, an Alliance MLA and chair of the Stormont assembly education committee.

“I want to thank all of the young campaigners who have been bravely raising their voices about this, and whose dedication will lead to seeing this wrong righted. The fact that in 2026 young girls and women had to campaign for this at all will not be forgotten.”

Substantial sums of public money were spent on drafting legislation to fix the minister’s error of judgment, Mathison added.

A girl’s right to wear trousers should not have been controversial, said Cathy Mason, a Sinn Féin MLA. “It should not have required further legislation from the education committee to force movement on something so basic.”

Cara Hunter, a Social Democratic and Labour party MLA, said young people who challenged the existing rules and refused to let the issue disappear deserved credit for the change. “The department must now deliver. This cannot be a right that exists on paper but becomes an argument at the school gate,” she said.
